test_texts:
[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Patient: Good morning, Doc. Thanks for fitting me into your schedule—it’s been pretty hectic lately.

Doctor: Good morning! No problem at all, always happy to see you. What brings you in today?

Patient: Honestly, there’s a bunch of little things. For starters, I just can’t seem to shake this cough. It’s not terrible, but it’s stubborn, and with my current workload stress, I wanted to make sure it’s nothing serious.

Doctor: How long have you had the cough? Any fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

Patient: I think it’s been going on for about two weeks. At first, I blamed it on staying up late—we’re in production for a new project and editing goes into the early hours. No fever, no pain, but I do sometimes feel slightly wheezy when I laugh or talk a lot, especially during our brainstorming sessions or read-throughs.

Doctor: Are you exposed to dust, chemicals, or any smoke while working?

Patient: Sometimes, yeah. We’ve been shooting on location, sometimes in older buildings, plus the guys in props occasionally use those fog machines. Plus, one of the stunts had some pyros—mostly safe, but that stuff lingers in the air.

Doctor: Thanks, that’s helpful. Are you working mostly indoors or outdoors?

Patient: Indoor for the most part, but we did a week out in the desert where I was constantly running between set and equipment trucks—lots of temperature shifts and wind.

Doctor: I see. Do you have any allergies that you know of? And do you smoke?

Patient: No, never smoked. As for allergies, my mom used to say I sneezed every time she cooked shrimp, but nothing severe that I know of. Maybe mild hay fever, but nothing that ever knocked me out of commission.

Doctor: Do you remember the last time you had something like this? Have you traveled recently?

Patient: Nothing this persistent. And yeah, actually—I flew from San Diego to New York last month for a training with the rest of my unit. It was right before principal shooting started, super tight schedule, and the air on planes always gets me.

Doctor: Has anyone around you been sick recently?

Patient: Half the crew got hit with colds. Craft services kept putting out massive trays of citrus, hoping vitamin C would help us out, but I still ended up with this cough.

Doctor: I can see why you’d want to be cautious. Has it affected your voice or energy levels on the job?

Patient: My voice, yeah—a little hoarse, which isn’t so great when I’m directing actors. My energy’s drained, too, but that’s not unusual after 18-hour days. As soon as we wrap, I try to get a nap in the trailer before I check in with the staff back at the base.

Doctor: When you say "base," are you referring to your work with the military, or is it a studio term?

Patient: Oh, both, actually. My main gig is producing, but I’m still with my reserve team. They like my “lead from the front” vibe, so I juggle production meetings with morning drills. Keeps me on my toes, but it also means sleep comes at a premium.

Doctor: That’s a demanding schedule. How are you managing stress?

Patient: I keep telling myself there’s a wrap party at the end of it. Jokes aside, I try mindfulness apps and call my parents most Sundays—sometimes they remind me to slow down, usually over the phone from back home or, if I’m lucky, over one of my mom’s homemade lumpia dinners.

Doctor: That sounds delicious. Do you have family nearby?

Patient: Not really. My folks are a state away now, but we try to stay connected. They always keep me grounded, especially with our family stories and some of the old Tagalog phrases sprinkled in conversations. Reminds me not to get lost in all the Hollywood chaos, you know?

Doctor: Absolutely, it’s so important to have those connections. You mentioned family meals—how’s your diet lately?

Patient: Could be better, Doc. I eat what’s available on set, which means way too many bagels and coffee. Whenever I can, I sneak home to make adobo or kare-kare, but mostly I’m at the mercy of the catering truck. Some days I miss the full rice cooker at family get-togethers.

Doctor: Are you able to get regular exercise with your schedule?

Patient: Besides running around wrangling cast and crew? Not as much structured exercise as I’d like. But my friends at the base have this unwritten rule—no skipping PT, even if I’m working late the night before. They’ll text me at dawn to make sure I show up. It’s a little brutal, but sometimes I think it’s the only thing keeping my joints in shape.

Doctor: That keeps you accountable! Any aches, other than feeling run down?

Patient: Lower back’s a bit tight, especially after dragging cables and lighting rigs. I was actually talking with one of the grips about swapping stretches—he’s an old hand on sets and knows all the tricks for not pulling things.

Doctor: Are you experiencing any joint swelling or weakness?

Patient: No swelling. Just a bit of stiffness in my right wrist—probably from holding the camera too long while doing that tracking shot last week. I tried using one of those compression sleeves, and it seemed to help.

Doctor: Have you had any issues with sleep, apart from being busy and tired?

Patient: Yeah, sleep is a mess. Between calls home, checking scripts, and the usual pre-dawn drills, I’m lucky if I get five hours. Sometimes I try to nap with headphones on, listening to OPM playlists or a recorded meditation. I probably need to unplug more.

Doctor: OPM? That helps you relax?

Patient: Original Pilipino Music, Doc! It’s what I grew up with. My dad always had it playing during Saturday cleaning. Even if I don’t always understand every word, it brings back a sense of home, kind of takes the edge off the stress.

Doctor: It’s great that you have that comfort. Any history of sleep disorders, like insomnia or sleep apnea in the family?

Patient: My uncle had sleep apnea, but for me, it’s just racing thoughts. I get a lot of emails from both coasts, sometimes even from overseas. The time zones make everything blur together.

Doctor: Understood. Let’s switch gears—are you taking any medications or supplements currently?

Patient: Just a daily multivitamin, and I threw some vitamin C in after one of my sergeants told me to. I try to drink turmeric tea when I can, thanks to my aunt’s advice. Other than that, nothing prescribed.

Doctor: Do you drink alcohol or use any recreational substances?

Patient: Rarely. The odd drink at wrap parties or when someone’s celebrating a promotion, but most of the time, I stay dry—strict rules from both jobs make that easy. Once in a while, I’ll indulge in a Red Horse with the crew after we finish a particularly tough shoot, but it’s not a habit.

Doctor: Any recent medical tests or annual check-ups?

Patient: Just last month, actually. I had a pretty thorough physical during my yearly assessment—it’s mandatory for my other gig. Lots of paperwork, vision and hearing checks, even got weighed in with the group. Docs said everything was fine, but I didn’t mention this cough.

Doctor: Were there any abnormalities in those tests? Cholesterol, blood pressure, glucose?

Patient: Nothing flagged. Blood pressure ticked up a bit, probably because I was running late, but no one seemed worried. I passed the run and strength test, so I guess I still have a little left in the tank.

Doctor: That’s excellent. Let’s talk about mental health. You’ve got a lot on your plate—how are you feeling emotionally?

Patient: It gets overwhelming, Doc. Some days I feel like I’m living out of my duffel, juggling scripts, call sheets, deployment schedules, and then there are calls home. I try to stay upbeat—got to keep morale high for both my crews—but the pressure can brew some anxiety.

Doctor: Do you find yourself ever feeling hopeless or losing interest in your usual hobbies?

Patient: Not hopeless. Honestly, when I get to watch a cut come together or see my squad succeed, I get this rush. It’s just the downtime that makes me restless. Like, I’ll start organizing my old collection of movie storyboards from college or try cooking sinigang just to feel grounded.

Doctor: Do you have anyone to talk to when it gets too much?

Patient: I’ve got a good network, thankfully. A few friends from my ROTC days check in, and my cousins have this group chat that never sleeps. Sometimes we talk about old times, sometimes about the latest action films—one of them even got a cameo on “Fresh Off the Boat.” Makes me smile.

Doctor: That’s wonderful, having that support. Has your mood ever interfered with your performance at work or with your duties elsewhere?

Patient: If anything, I push myself harder so it doesn’t. But there are days when the exhaustion hits and it’s easy to snap at someone for being late or missing a cue. I always apologize after—it’s not how I like to lead, whether it’s on set or with my team.

Doctor: Have you considered speaking with a counselor?

Patient: There’s a counselor we’re allowed to see through our rotation—it’s encouraged, actually. Haven’t taken advantage yet, but a buddy of mine says it helps. I’ll think about it, if things get heavier.

Doctor: That’s a good option to have. You’re juggling a lot, and it’s good to seek support before things build up. Are you currently concerned about anything specific—health, work, home life?

Patient: The main concern is just not dropping the ball. My unit expects a lot, and the folks funding our project don’t tolerate delays. Add in making time to call my lola back home, and it’s a balancing act.

Doctor: You mentioned your lola—do you keep in touch regularly?

Patient: I try, as much as the time difference allows. She’s back in the Philippines, so I’m always recalculating when’s a good time to call. She’s big on sharing family stories—like how she watched her youngest cross a huge ocean so many years ago, taking pride in every milestone her grandkids reach over here.

Doctor: That sounds really meaningful. Do you visit back there often?

Patient: Not as often as I’d like, but every few years I make the trip. The last time, it was for a cousin’s wedding—lots of lechon, karaoke, old photo albums. Seeing the old school where my parents met was something special. I always bring back pasalubong for everyone—it’s expected.

Doctor: It’s wonderful to stay connected to your roots. Is there any history of chronic diseases in your family I should be aware of?

Patient: Dad’s side has some high blood pressure, mom’s side has a bit of diabetes, though everyone’s mostly healthy these days—lots of fish and veggies in their diet. I keep an eye out, just in case.

Doctor: When you travel overseas, do you take any specific health precautions?

Patient: Always check if I need shots—my military doc hounds me about it. I’m the one on set prepared with a first aid kit, partly out of habit from training, partly because you just never know what might happen on location.

Doctor: That’s good practice. Do you handle medical emergencies on set since you’ve had formal training?

Patient: Yeah, sometimes. I’ve patched up more scraped knees and minor burns than I can count, and when someone fainted last month during a long take, I kept things calm until the ambulance arrived. Comes with the territory, I suppose.

Doctor: Sounds like you handle stress well in the moment. Does your work have regular health and safety briefings?

Patient: Absolutely. We start every shoot day with a rundown. I even lead a few; my experience sort of makes it my ‘other hat’ besides organizing scripts and calling shots.

Doctor: Are you happy with your current health overall, or are there things you’d like to change in your lifestyle?

Patient: If I could tweak something, it’d be slowing down to have more proper meals and more normal sleep. Maybe more family time—my dad always says “don’t forget where you started” whenever I mention another late night at the lot. And someday, I’d love to direct a film back in Manila.

Doctor: Those are great goals. Based on everything you’ve shared, your cough is likely from a combination of exhaustion, exposure, and possibly dry air. I’ll listen to your lungs and check you over, just to be thorough, but I think you’ll be back at full strength with some rest. I’d also encourage those support systems—keep those video calls, stay close with family, and don’t be afraid to see the counselor if you need to.

Patient: Thanks, Doc. I appreciate that. Sometimes it’s easy to forget to ask for help with so much to get done, but I’ll take your advice. I know my squad and my crew both count on me, but I know when to listen to the person in charge—and today, that’s you.

Doctor: Thank you! You’re doing a lot, and you have every reason to be proud. Let’s get you checked, and if everything’s clear, I’ll write up some recommendations for managing your cough and improving sleep. Feel free to reach out if anything gets worse.

Patient: Will do. And if you ever need someone to yell “action” for a health video, you know who to call.

Doctor: I might take you up on that offer! Let’s take a listen to those lungs.
[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Patient: Good morning, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me. I’m not really sure where to start, but I thought it was time for a check-up. Been a while, actually.

Doctor: Good morning! No problem at all, it’s great that you’ve come in. Is there anything in particular you’ve been concerned about, or is this more of a general wellness visit?

Patient: More general, I guess. Now that things have settled down a bit for me, figured I shouldn’t ignore my health. I was feeling a little wiped out last week, but it’s probably just this dreary mud season messing with me. Weather up here really doesn’t do me any favors.

Doctor: That’s understandable, these transition periods between winter and spring in the north can really drag folks down. When you say wiped out, do you mean tired, short of breath, anything else?

Patient: Mostly tired, and muscles kind of achy. I notice it when I walk up the hills near my place, little things tire me out. No fever or cough, though. Ever since maple sugaring started up on the trails again, I’ve tried to keep active, but it’s not been easy.

Doctor: How long has this been going on?

Patient: On and off for the past month, honestly. I didn’t pay much attention—frankly, with my schedule, every day blends together a bit.

Doctor: And your appetite—has that changed at all?

Patient: It’s about the same. I still have my coffee and toast for breakfast. Lunch is hit or miss, and I make myself dinner most nights. Sometimes, I put off making a meal just because I’m not very hungry, but other times I’ll snack late at night. I chalk it up to missing the company I used to have at dinner.

Doctor: Understood. Any significant weight changes?

Patient: I dropped a bit, maybe five pounds since last fall, but didn’t think much of it. I keep busy puttering around the house and tending to the tiny garden I started this year. Sometimes I just forget to eat when I’m in the middle of things.

Doctor: You mentioned missing your dinner company—have there been any major changes in your social life lately?

Patient: Well, it’s just me at home now, unless you count the dog. My friends are scattered, and my daughter lives out west, so it gets pretty quiet. I suppose I’ve had to get used to that over the last few years. No more big Sunday meals with the family, and these days, it’s more frozen stew and reruns in the evening.

Doctor: That transition can be hard for many people. Have you been feeling lonely or low in mood?

Patient: Some days are harder than others. Still, I find comfort in traditions, like dancing at the circle when I can catch a ride down to one of our gatherings. That helps a bit—at least it reminds me of home and growing up with my cousins, all the stories and songs we shared.

Doctor: That sounds wonderful. Are these events something you attend often?

Patient: When I can. There aren’t many nearby groups who keep it going up here, but every once in a while, someone organizes a get-together, or my cousin from Tucson sends me videos of the dances we used to do as kids. Sometimes I try to cook the same fry bread she makes, though it never turns out quite the same.

Doctor: That connection can be very meaningful, especially being far from your roots. Have you been able to keep in touch with your family back home?

Patient: I do, over the phone mostly. My aunts send me pictures of the fiestas, and I see my cousins’ kids in their regalia. It warms me up a bit, even if I can’t be there in person. Haven’t been able to travel out to the desert for ceremonies—a little tough with the airfare and my current situation.

Doctor: It’s good that you try and stay connected. Let’s talk a bit about your day-to-day. Are you working or retired now?

Patient: Oh, those workdays are done for me. I clocked out for the last time a good while ago. Doesn’t feel quite like retirement, more like on a never-ending vacation that never got properly planned. My mornings are quiet, and some days I lose track of time just tending to what needs fixing around the place or hanging out at the library.

Doctor: And do you find that your days have enough structure to them, or would you prefer to be doing something different?

Patient: I like keeping to myself for the most part. I spent enough years running after someone else’s schedule, so a bit of solitude isn’t all bad. Every once in a while, I volunteer at the food pantry—just a couple days a month now, if they need the help. Otherwise, it’s just my dog, the Red Sox on the radio, and the peepers out by the marsh.

Doctor: Sounds peaceful, but sometimes too much quiet can take its toll. Do you have support from friends or neighbors?

Patient: My neighbor, Irene, checks in on me—she brings me those whoopie pies from the bakery in Concord. She’s a lifesaver, really. Folks here are mostly friendly if a bit reserved. Not like the busy crowds back where I grew up. Sometimes I do miss the old days—family dinners, backyard bonfires, that sort of thing. But everyone goes their separate ways, I suppose. I’ve learned to get by with just me.

Doctor: Did you grow up in a busy household?

Patient: Oh yes. There were so many of us, my mother used to say she couldn’t keep track. Summers, we’d all pile in to go fishing on the river, and winters, we listened to stories around the fire. Most of my early years were filled with ceremonies and shared meals, always someone to play with or look after. It’s quieter now. Most of my childhood friends are still out west or down on the border.

Doctor: That sense of community can be hard to replace, but you seem to carry those memories fondly. Let’s shift to some routine health questions—have you had any chest pain, palpitations, or breathing difficulties?

Patient: No, nothing like that. Blood pressure’s been good, I think. I take what the last doc prescribed. I try to remember my morning meds—keeping them all straight got easier once my daughter mailed me that pill sorter. She used to be the boss in the house, keeping my mornings on track.

Doctor: May I ask what medications you are currently taking?

Patient: Lisinopril for pressure, and a baby aspirin each day. I refill them every other month, make the drive out east to the pharmacy when they call me. Getting around here isn’t always easy, not with the town so spread out. At least the views of the Whites make the drive worth it sometimes.

Doctor: Absolutely. Do you take any herbal supplements or over-the-counter medicines?

Patient: Once in a while, I make tea from the chamomile my cousin sends me. She says it’s good for calming the nerves—helps me sleep when the nor’easters keep me up. No other pills.

Doctor: How’s your sleep overall? Any difficulty falling or staying asleep?

Patient: I get to sleep easy—might be the dog curling up next to me or the sound of the owl outside my window. Sometimes nightmares catch me, things from the past I’d rather forget, but they come less often now. It’s the early mornings that get to me. As soon as the sun’s up, I’m awake, can’t seem to sleep in like I did when I was younger.

Doctor: How about caffeine or alcohol consumption?

Patient: One cup of coffee in the morning, and that’s about it. Used to drink more, but after the split, I decided to cut back. No sense keeping wine on the shelf when I’m the only one around. Doc, I don’t think I’ve bought a bottle since the paperwork was final.

Doctor: Do you ever feel like the past affects your mood or your day-to-day life?

Patient: Sometimes. Those memories can bring a smile or sting a bit. I had 15 years of making things work, and while I don’t regret the time, it’s behind me now. Learned to enjoy the quiet—mostly. I do miss the laughter sometimes.

Doctor: That’s completely understandable. Everyone processes changes in their own time. Let’s discuss your physical activity. Besides your walks and tending the garden, do you do any other form of exercise?

Patient: I try to stretch every morning—old habits I picked up from watching my uncle. He showed me this shoulder move to keep my joints from stiffening up. Sometimes, when the mood strikes, I’ll put on some music and remember the old dances. Good for the soul and the bones—or so my grandmother used to say.

Doctor: Are you experiencing any joint pain or swelling?

Patient: Bit of stiffness in my knees when the cold rolls in. Pretty typical for this time of year, though—I’ve gotten used to it. I try to keep moving, but shoveling the driveway is a young person’s game. These granite hills aren’t getting any smoother for my feet either.

Doctor: Do you have any family history of chronic diseases like diabetes, heart disease, or high cholesterol?

Patient: Diabetes runs in my family—my father struggled with it for years. Saw a lot of my aunties dealing with heart trouble too. We come from people who loved their stews and fry bread a bit too much, if you know what I mean. I keep an eye on my numbers, and try to listen when my daughter lectures me about carbs.

Doctor: Have you ever been screened for diabetes yourself?

Patient: Yes, last time I went to the big hospital in Lebanon—just before the snows set in last year. Bloodwork came back fine, though the doc said I should cut down on sweets. Not easy with the kind of desserts floating around the sugar shacks each spring.

Doctor: I can imagine! I see here you marked a box about tobacco—are you currently smoking or using any products like that?

Patient: No tobacco. Haven’t touched it in ages. Used to, but I quit around the same time I figured out living alone wasn’t the curse I thought it would be. It made a difference—my breathing’s not what it once was, but I feel better for it.

Doctor: Excellent, that’s great to hear. How about routine screenings—when was your last colonoscopy or mammogram?

Patient: Last colonoscopy was two, maybe three, years back. Drove all the way into Manchester for that one—long day but worth it to check things out. Mammogram was last fall, when the local clinic offered those free screenings. Everything came back clean.

Doctor: Perfect, it sounds like you’re up to date. Do you get your flu shot annually?

Patient: Always. Between my daughter’s nagging and my cousin’s reminders, I never miss it. With the kind of winters we have here, safe is better than sorry.

Doctor: Excellent. Since you mentioned spending time at home, have you experienced any trouble with balance or falls recently?

Patient: Only once this winter—I slipped on some ice trying to get the paper. Got up with just a bruised ego, thankfully. Irene across the street saw it and came over with her cane, just to be sure. I try to be careful; the last thing I need is a hip out of place.

Doctor: Safety is important, especially with all that black ice you get up here. Any vision or hearing problems you’ve noticed?

Patient: Eyes are starting to have trouble in low light. Glasses help, but some nights I just stick with the big print books from the library. Hearing’s not what it was when I was running to catch the bus as a kid, but I get by. If the TV’s too low, the dog lets me know something’s off.

Doctor: I see. Have you had your eyes and hearing checked recently?

Patient: Eyes, yes, just last summer in Concord. Hearing, not since they did that quick test during my annual. Maybe due for another one. Guessing it’ll just confirm what I already know—I’m not getting any younger.

Doctor: That’s true for all of us! Tell me a bit more about your daily routine—do you drive yourself places, or rely on someone else?

Patient: Still drive, mostly. Try to avoid it when the roads are bad, but as long as there’s no snow or flooding from the big melt, I manage fine. If it’s a long trip, sometimes Irene tags along. There’s not much in the way of buses out here. Not like in the cities.

Doctor: Understood. How about insurance coverage—are you comfortable with your current health plan?

Patient: I’ve been with the same insurer for years—comes with a few headaches, but nothing too bad. There was a paperwork mix-up once, but I called their toll-free, and the woman on the other end helped me sort it out. She had a familiar accent, reminded me a bit of home.

Doctor: Thank you for sharing all of that. Before we wrap up, anything else on your mind, any concerns about medications, memory, or new symptoms?

Patient: Not really. I just want to stay healthy enough to catch the powwow the next time it makes its way up to the Green. Those have always felt like coming home to me—even if it means driving a couple of hours into Vermont or Maine. Just being able to take part, hear the songs and taste the food, that’s more medicine than anything I get in a bottle these days.

Doctor: That’s a wonderful goal. I’ll make sure we keep you in good shape for it. I’ll set up your routine labs, and we’ll check your blood pressure and make sure you’re up to date with everything else. If you ever need to talk more about your mood or anything else, please don’t hesitate to come in.

Patient: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate you listening. It’s good to know I’ve got someone here to check in with—especially on the days when the mountain fog just won’t lift.

Doctor: Of course. I’m always here. Take care, and enjoy those spring peepers! Let me know if you need anything before your next appointment.

Patient: Will do. Have a good one, Doctor.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

Other: Yep, you’re coming through fine. Thanks for jumping on, I know your schedule’s packed. How’s your week going?

Target: It’s been good, though a bit overwhelming—everyone’s rushing to finalize their Q1 reports before the month wraps up, so you know how it is. I feel like my life has just become a whirlwind of expense ledgers and double-checking spreadsheets for tiny mismatches, and we’re not even at tax season’s peak yet.

Other: Welcome to the world of finance, right? I remember those days when working in audits—sometimes it felt like the numbers never stopped rolling in. But hey, at least you’re lucky enough to work with variety, right? Not every client’s the same.

Target: For sure, and with this job I get to see so many different business stories just from their ledgers. Though, honestly, I’m probably not the typical accountant most people picture—not just crunching numbers but kind of stuck in between worlds in a way. Maybe that’s why I got into this in the first place. I’m used to weaving between perspectives.

Other: That’s interesting! What do you mean about weaving between worlds? Is it something you picked up growing up?

Target: Pretty much. Both my mom and dad come from different backgrounds, so at home there was always this blend of traditions. Some days my grandma would cook cornbread, and the next it’d be dumplings or tamales. No two family reunions looked alike—sometimes the music was jazz, sometimes mariachi, and sometimes both blaring at the same time. I can count on one hand the people at my school with the same sort of mix.

Other: That must have made you a pro at navigating balance early on! Did you ever find that influenced how you approach things in the office, especially when dealing with tricky clients or tricky figures?

Target: Absolutely. Having that sort of background forces you to read a room quickly and bridge gaps, whether it’s in culture or in numbers. Sometimes I’m the only one on the team who knows how to make everyone agree on something, because I know how to translate between different expectations. 

Other: I wish we had more of that in our own department. Lots of straight lines, if you know what I mean. Hard to get folks to meet in the middle sometimes. Speaking of—how did you end up in this field so young? Most of my colleagues did the whole college and years of training before coming near the books.

Target: Well, I started a bit ahead of the curve, at least for my age—I had to. High school offered an accounting elective, which honestly saved me. It was more interesting than any lit class and way less intimidating than algebra. I started part-time with a local accountant after school—he took a risk on me, maybe because his daughter was in my math class—and then things just kept rolling from there.

Other: That’s impressive! So you managed to jump ahead and get some hands-on experience while most folks your age were still figuring themselves out.

Target: Yeah, tell me about it. Sometimes when I’m in meetings and realize most of the people around the table expect me to talk about prom and football games, not 401(k)’s and asset statements, it’s a little odd. The thing no one really knows is that I actually haven’t finished school yet. I’m in that year where people start learning to drive. Most of my friends are still prepping for their PSATs, not their client reviews.

Other: Wait, wow—you mean you’re still in high school? That’s... that’s impressive. You don’t meet many sophomores working the numbers in asset management.

Target: Yeah, sophomore. Whenever someone asks how I manage tax season and homework, I just shrug and say it’s about prioritizing, but really, I just love the work. Math classes feel less stressful when you’re balancing someone’s payroll on the side.

Other: You must have had a head for numbers from early on then. And parents who support your own ambitions, I’d guess.

Target: For sure, and an older cousin who would help me with my first spreadsheets, way back in middle school. My parents never had to worry about my grades, just how many hours I was logging at the desk instead of outside. It probably helps that I was always here, rather than moving around—never had to get used to new schools, just the new teachers coming in each year.

Other: Born and bred here, huh? So you’ve always had that local vibe.

Target: Yeah. Even my birth certificate looks almost boring, it’s so normal—no international stamps or anything. All the schools I went to, the places where I’ve worked internships, everything’s been within the same city limits. I’ve never had to worry about filling out forms that ask about where I was born. 

Other: That probably made things simpler for starting work early, right? Some of those regulatory forms are a nightmare if you weren’t. How do you handle the age thing at work—do folks take you seriously?

Target: Sometimes it’s tough to be taken seriously, especially when a client realizes I’m not even old enough to vote yet. I remember last year someone tried to hand out drinks at a celebration party, and HR stepped in fast—let’s just say I was jokingly awarded “Best ID Under 18.” But if you’re good at what you do, the right people notice, age aside.

Other: Being the youngest in the room can give you an edge—fresh ideas, but also fresh perspective. Out of curiosity, does your birthday ever fall during those hectic financial periods?

Target: Actually, my birthday always falls during the longest lull every year, right before everyone gets antsy about daylight savings and spring numbers. It’s funny, because as a kid, I always associated it with stuffing my face on cake and then a week later trying to figure out what to give up for Lent at church.

Other: That puts your birthday sometime late February then, with Lent right after… 

Target: Right, I’m always seeing those "happy birthday" messages right about the time folks start buying Valentine’s clearance. This year was a small one—just a dozen people from work, a couple friends from my old study group, and I got to eat way too much red velvet. And there was an accounting joke on my cake, of course.

Other: So, you’re what, just turned 17?

Target: Yep, seventeen just a couple months ago. I’m in that strange stage where half the kids my age are dreaming about finally getting wheels and I’m staring at forms about tax audits and payroll compliance. I do still have to fit homework in between all my balance sheets, though.

Other: That’s incredible. And balancing high school with your work in finance seems like a juggling act. Are your teachers supportive?

Target: Most are, though some just shake their heads and try to keep me from zoning out in algebra. I had to convince the principal that my missing some team assemblies for work stuff was actually worth it. One of the counselors started calling me "the numbers kid" and now the nickname’s kind of stuck.

Other: It sounds like your drive and adaptability set you apart, honestly. Do you ever feel like you’re missing out on anything by not taking the traditional path through school?

Target: Sometimes—most of my classmates are prepping for the dance or the next football game, and I’m focused on closing ledgers before our client site visits. I wish I had more time to just relax, or maybe to join one of the robotics clubs. But the trade-off is, I’m getting to build a career before most of my friends even choose a college major. And home’s always a mix of music and food from all over, which helps me feel less out of sync.

Other: You clearly embrace the richness of your family’s background. Do you ever get questions about your identity from coworkers, or do you keep that private?

Target: People are usually curious when I mention that my celebrations are a little bit of everything—like one year, my mom set up an altar for Día de los Muertos at the same time as my dad tried to get us all to watch the Rose Parade. Sometimes I see people trying to figure out where I “fit,” but honestly, I’ve gotten good at just being myself and letting them draw their own conclusions.

Other: That’s a wonderful attitude. It sounds like you bring a layered perspective to any team you join. And going back to your career—do you see yourself specializing more in audits or something else in finance?

Target: Audits have that puzzle-solving edge I love, but I’m interested in branching out—maybe forensic accounting, tracking down numbers that don’t add up for a bigger reason. There’s something thrilling about seeing a spreadsheet that looks right at first but knowing there’s a story under the surface.

Other: Sounds like you’re already thinking ahead, which makes sense for someone who started young. Have your family been able to support you with all these ambitions?

Target: They have, even if sometimes all they understand about what I do is “check the math.” But they’re good at reminding me to take pride in every part of who I am—whether that’s following family recipes, speaking some Spanish with my uncle or playing dominoes with my other grandma. Kind of fitting that half our extended family reunions are a little United Nations, honestly.

Other: So in the middle of all the numbers, you still get to stay connected to both sides of your heritage. Must make holidays pretty exciting when you’re mixing so many traditions.

Target: It does! Lunar New Year turns into a fusion with Mardi Gras at our house—my little cousins running around with red envelopes and beads, and my aunt insisting we eat black-eyed peas and dumplings. It keeps things interesting and makes me proud to bring a bit of that to work, even if it’s just sharing a homemade snack now and then in the break room.

Other: That’s fantastic. With all the family and career commitments, do you ever plan to pursue a college degree later, or do you think real-world experience will keep you moving forward?

Target: Honestly, I feel like there’s still a lot to learn before I even think about college. Seeing classmates talk about campus visits makes me wonder if I’m missing out, but the work I do now is teaching me things that school can’t. Maybe down the line, I’ll look at a degree, but right now I’m just focusing on getting through sophomore year and not letting the midterms get too far out of hand.

Other: It’s refreshing to hear you’re keeping your options open. Sometimes, not fitting the expected mold creates the best opportunities. Do your coworkers ever notice your energy stands out?

Target: Some do, especially when they find out my music taste is all over the place—from salsa to blues to old Motown. I actually DJ’d the last office holiday party, which was hilarious since I had to play half current hits and half throwbacks for the partners. I guess it shows I’m used to juggling a lot at once.

Other: Sounds like you’re as good at mixing beats as you are at mixing spreadsheets! Before we wrap up, any advice you’d give to someone who finds themselves in between worlds, whether in culture or in career, the way you have?

Target: I’d say—learn to take pride in having more than one story to tell. Whether that’s at home or at work, don’t let people box you in. Use it, because it gives you more ways to solve problems and connect with others. And don’t worry if your path doesn’t match what textbooks say—a nontraditional road sometimes leads to the best destinations, even if you have to balance client calls with calculus homework.

Other: That’s wise beyond your years, seriously. Thank you for sharing your story today. I’ve actually got a couple of colleagues who could use your perspective—I hope you won’t mind if I mention your experience, without naming names, of course.

Target: No problem at all. If it helps someone else see themselves in the work, I’d be all for it. And if anyone needs tips on surviving back-to-back deadlines and geometry quizzes, send them my way.

Other: Will do! Thanks again for taking the time, and for being so open. Let’s touch base again once the quarter closes. I’m sure you’ll have plenty of new tales by then.

Target: Looking forward to it! Have a great rest of your week. And good luck with your own audits.

Other: Thanks, you too. Talk soon.

test_texts:
[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Patient: Good morning, Doctor. Thanks for squeezing me in before your lunch break. I know you’re super busy.

Doctor: Not a problem at all. It’s always good to see you. What brings you in today?

Patient: Well, I guess it’s a combination of things. I’ve had these random headaches for a while, and they’re sort of messing with my focus at the factory. Plus, with everything at home and at work, I just feel pretty worn out most days.

Doctor: I'm sorry to hear that. Let's try to sort things out. How long have these headaches been going on, and can you describe them for me? Are they sharp, dull, or does it vary?

Patient: They started maybe two or three months ago. They’re not sharp, more like this dull ache that creeps up, especially after my shift. Sometimes it feels like someone wrapped a rubber band around my head. The days I’m standing at my station for too long, it gets worse, but it doesn’t always go away with painkillers.

Doctor: Do you notice if they come on at a particular time of day, or when doing a certain task?

Patient: Usually in the afternoons, right after lunch, but sometimes later too. We’re always on our feet, putting together small parts at the assembly line. They changed our schedule recently, so now I do more repetitive motions, sometimes with heavier materials. Maybe that’s messing with me as well.

Doctor: Got it. Any changes in your vision, nausea, or sensitivity to light or noise when the headaches happen?

Patient: Sometimes the lights at work bug me, especially the flickering ones. I get a bit queasy if I’m on my feet too long, but that’s probably from skipping breaks. My crew lead always forgets, you know?

Doctor: That’s important to note. How are things going outside of work? You mentioned feeling worn out “with everything at home”—is there more stress recently?

Patient: Yeah. My other half’s job just cut his hours, so we’ve been juggling bills, and I pick up double shifts where I can. Plus, honestly, managing the house, trying to keep food on the table—sometimes it gets to be a lot. There’s not much downtime, especially since I help my niece with her homework in the evenings.

Doctor: It sounds like you carry a lot of responsibility, both at work and at home. Are you able to get any rest or time for yourself? How’s your sleep been?

Patient: I wish. By the time I can sit down, it’s usually past eleven. And then my brain just seems to go a mile a minute, thinking about what needs to be done the next day. On a good night, I’ll get five or six hours, but some nights I’m up watching late-night TV repeats—my husband snores anyway, so even when I do fall asleep, it’s kind of light.

Doctor: I see. Sleep deprivation can definitely contribute to headaches and feeling exhausted. On the weekends, do you get a chance to rest more, or is it just as busy?

Patient: It’s a bit better. We used to go out on Saturday nights, but now we mostly stay home. Sometimes I’ll have a cookout with family for special days—like, last summer, my anniversary lined up really close with the fireworks in town. It was fun, even if it was just the two of us and a couple friends.

Doctor: That sounds lovely. How many years have you and your partner been married?

Patient: Just over a year and a half—feels longer some days and way shorter on others! We actually tied the knot not too long ago, small courthouse thing, just before all the big changes happened at work.

Doctor: Congratulations to you both. Let’s talk a little about your work. You said you’re on your feet assembling parts—is that mostly manual work, or do you operate machinery too?

Patient: Mostly manual. Some folks get assigned the fancy machines, but I’m one of the folks who snaps together the little plastic and metal bits. Sometimes I have to use a small handheld press, but nothing huge. My station has containers of random parts, and I follow the diagrams, popping them together over and over. If I get that wrong, it gets sent back down the line—nobody is happy about that.

Doctor: That sounds repetitive, which can be hard on the body. Any pain in your wrists or hands? Numbness or tingling?

Patient: Oh, for sure. Especially in my right hand. It’s like after eight hours, my fingers are stiff, and sometimes my wrist feels like it has pins and needles. They told us to stretch, but no one really stops to do it with the line moving so fast. Plus, I help clean up at the end of the night—someone’s gotta pick up all the stray screws and pieces.

Doctor: I’ll share some stretches and tips that might help with the hands and wrists before you finish today. Do you have time to eat during your shift, or do you skip meals?

Patient: It depends. I grab what I can from the vending machine—usually chips or a candy bar. Sometimes I pack a sandwich but forget it, or someone else eats it by accident. The break room can get crowded, and if you’re at the back of the line, you barely have ten minutes.

Doctor: Nutrition could be playing a part in how you’re feeling. We can go over some quick snack ideas that are better for your energy and focus, even on a tight schedule.

Patient: That would be great. Sometimes I think if I’d finished school, maybe I’d have a desk job instead of being on the line, but I left high school before graduation to start working. In my family, that’s kind of the usual. Everyone starts earning as soon as they can, and you just keep at it.

Doctor: It sounds like you’ve worked very hard for a long time, and your experience is valuable. If you’re ever interested in night classes or other opportunities, I can recommend community programs that don’t require a full diploma.

Patient: Thanks, Doctor, maybe someday. For now, work’s work, and there’s bills to pay. Sometimes I wish I'd pushed through that last year, but back then, it felt like I needed to help out at home more.

Doctor: Are you feeling any pressure from managers at the job, or do you feel supported?

Patient: It depends on who’s covering the shift. One supervisor is always hovering, counting how many units we finish every hour. That stress piles up, especially if you’re tired. But some coworkers are nice, and we look out for each other. It helps keep me going. My hands would fall off if I didn't have people to joke around with.

Doctor: Social support is important. Do you ever talk with any of your coworkers about what you're feeling—like about the stress, or even the headaches?

Patient: Sometimes. A couple of us band together and complain in the parking lot before our rides show up. One of the older ladies says she’s had headaches since forever, but she says it’s just “part of the job” and to drink more coffee. Not sure that helps! My spouse has been good about reminding me to rest, but sometimes I don’t listen.

Doctor: How about your periods—have there been any changes? Sometimes headaches can be connected to hormonal shifts.

Patient: They’re regular, as always. I don’t have any unusual pain, just the normal cramps. My aunt used to joke that in our family, we all get a visit from “Aunt Flo” the week after those big summer parades, and for me, it’s always been true.

Doctor: That’s helpful to know. Has anyone in your family had migraines or similar issues?

Patient: My mom used to say she’d get them around her birthday—which is funny, because mine is just a few days after hers. She always celebrated at the big Fourth of July cookouts, and so did I growing up. My friends would tease that the whole town set off fireworks for me, since I was usually the youngest at the party by a few months.

Doctor: So, your birthday must fall right around the holiday?

Patient: Yep, always had fireworks for my birthday. Makes it easy to remember, even if you forget the cake!

Doctor: That's a fun tradition! You mentioned your mom’s headaches—did she ever get treatment for those?

Patient: No, she always just took over-the-counter stuff and said it’d pass. She ran the house with four kids, so I guess she just powered through. I’m trying not to be like that—figured it was time to get checked out properly before I ignore it too long.

Doctor: That's a good decision. Preventive care is important, and we don't want things to get worse. Out of curiosity, how old are you now?

Patient: I turned twenty last summer. Still feels weird not being a teen anymore, but here we are! My friends joked I finally joined the “adult club” last year, but the only thing that changed was I got more bills.

Doctor: You’re still young, and you’ve got a lot on your plate. Since you said you do mostly manual work and are on your feet all day, do you notice any swelling in your legs or feet?

Patient: Sometimes. After a double, my ankles get puffy, but it goes away when I prop them up at night. I heard one of my coworkers talk about compression socks—do those really help?

Doctor: They can be very helpful when standing or walking for long hours. I can suggest a few options for you to try. Also, making a point to move your feet up and down while you’re standing can help pump the blood back up toward your heart.

Patient: I’ll try that. I just want to make sure I’m healthy enough to keep working. My husband worries I’m burning myself out, but I tell him that’s what marriage is sometimes—looking out for each other, picking up the slack. He helps when he can, but I’m usually the one with the steadier paycheck.

Doctor: Having a partner who cares is very important, especially when things are stressful. Are you both able to talk about your health concerns openly with each other?

Patient: Oh, for sure. We’re pretty open about that stuff. He jokingly calls himself my “unofficial nurse” and always checks if I’ve eaten or if I remembered my asthma inhaler.

Doctor: That’s excellent support. Speaking of which—any changes with your breathing, or have your asthma symptoms changed?

Patient: Not really. The only time it acts up is if someone decides to break out the cleaning sprays at work, or if a machine gets too dusty. I haven’t needed to use my rescue inhaler more than once in the last couple of weeks.

Doctor: Good to hear you’re managing it well. With the headaches, your work environment, and everything else, I think we should do some basic bloodwork, maybe check your iron and general health. How does that sound?

Patient: That’s fine. Needles don’t scare me—my niece hates them, but I’m the family “tough girl.” Just as long as I don’t have to miss work for too long.

Doctor: The nurse can draw blood today and you’ll be in and out quickly. I’ll also refer you to an occupational health specialist who may have some tips specific to your work environment. Let’s keep following up on how you’re feeling, especially with those headaches.

Patient: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate you listening. It means a lot—not everyone takes the time, especially when you’re “just another worker” from the factory floor.

Doctor: You’re never just another worker here. Your health and well-being matter. Reach out anytime, especially if you notice new symptoms between now and your next appointment.

Patient: Will do. Maybe I’ll finally get more sleep if I can convince my husband to get that anti-snore mouthguard you mentioned last time!

Doctor: It's worth a try! Take care, and let’s see you back soon for those results.

Patient: Thank you. Have a good day, Doctor.

Doctor: You too. Take care.

test_texts:
[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Target: Hi there, thanks for hopping on this call. I know Mondays are always busy, so I appreciate you making the time.

Other: No problem at all! I actually just had a lull between meetings, so it's perfect. How’s everything at the branch this morning?

Target: Well, it’s steady so far. Typical start to the week: folks lining up first thing to get their deposits in. I had the usual rush of customers with weekend cash to drop off, and then the regulars coming in to ask about their statements. Nothing too out of the ordinary—although that ancient coin collector came in again and wanted to chat about rare quarters for almost half an hour.

Other: Oh, I know exactly who you mean! He’s got some stories, that’s for sure. Do you get to interact with him often?

Target: Pretty often. I think he likes that I've always got a smile for him. Plus, I’m basically a fixture there now, since I’ve been working up front for a few years. Some people think being behind a glass window all day is dull, but honestly, I like it. You get to know the customers, and there’s a rhythm to it.

Other: That’s a good attitude! I admire anyone who can keep that energy when they’re handling everyone’s cash and keeping all those numbers straight. Has the system been behaving? I heard the software upgrade last week gave a few people headaches.

Target: Oh, tell me about it. We rolled out the update last Tuesday, and the balancing process at the end of the day took twice as long. There was one moment where I thought I was going to be at my window past seven, but I figured it out. A bit of patience, a double-check, and some caffeine later, and everything reconciled in time.

Other: You’ve always been meticulous, that much I know. I guess your faculty advisor back in college would be proud.

Target: Well, I hope so! Those days hammering out Excel assignments and group presentations taught me a lot. I still remember my final year project— analyzing data from small businesses. Oddly, it helped more than I expected when talking people through their savings and business accounts now.

Other: Funny how that works out. It’s not everyone who comes in with that kind of foundation, especially for front-line roles. Did you always know you wanted to work in a financial setting, or was it a happy accident?

Target: Kind of a combination. My first job was more of a necessity—just something to pay the bills during my last semester. But after graduation, the bank needed a full-timer at the desk, and I was in the right place at the right time. I think my attention to detail just fit. Besides, I come from a family where balancing the checkbook was a monthly ritual. I guess it rubbed off on me.

Other: I can relate! My mother still keeps paper ledgers. Makes me smile thinking about it. I’m curious: have you thought about moving up? You’ve got the degree, and you handle the pressure well.

Target: Sometimes. You know, when you’re the person actually counting the bills and handling deposits day after day, you get to see how the branch operates. Management sometimes tries to convince me to look at assistant manager roles, but I like the daily connection you make at the windows. It’s a pretty unique space, and people trust you with their livelihoods.

Other: Makes sense. Trust is huge, especially where you are.

Target: Yeah. There was this woman—she came in last week, nervous because she was opening her first account ever. I walked her through each step slowly. Reminded me a little of college orientation day, honestly. New people, new systems, trying to make it not so overwhelming for them.

Other: Have you picked up any interesting stories working with customers for so long?

Target: Oh, plenty. I’ve heard about everything from grandchildren learning to save to big lottery winners who are suddenly overwhelmed by all the attention. One time, a customer brought in a cake for my birthday in the middle of the summer—it caught me completely off guard. I don’t think I’ve ever had so much of the staff singing at once, except maybe the holiday party.

Other: That must have been a sight! Was it a milestone birthday?

Target: Not a big one. Actually, last year marked a quarter century for me, so it was a good excuse for cake at least. The funny part is, my birthday always falls right around that time at the end of July when everyone on the team is itching for summer vacation, so it’s easy for it to slip by quietly.

Other: Oh, end of July—great time to have a birthday! You can always celebrate it outside. Plus, you just missed Leo season—or are you one?

Target: Right in the thick of it. Never too hot for ice cream, I’ll say that.

Other: So, you’re 26 now, right?

Target: Yeah, just hit it last year. It’s strange thinking about it—seeing people my age bringing in graduation checks for their siblings, remembering what that felt like not so long ago.

Other: That’s awesome. I love hearing when people from the younger generation stick with a job and make it their own. You started working at the branch right after college, yes?

Target: Yep, just a couple of months after university. Undergrad days feel both recent and far off at the same time. It’s funny, I was only 19 when I started college, and then suddenly, I’m the one showing new hires the ropes. Life comes at you quick.

Other: Time flies. You ever miss campus life?

Target: Sometimes, yeah. I miss cramming for tests with friends, or late-night debates about which cafeteria had the best pizza. Not so much the student loans, though—I picked a state school to keep my debt low. Oddly enough, the paperwork I learned to fill out for those loans prepped me to help people with forms now.

Other: Ha, I love that. It always cracks me up how the little things from school end up making a difference here. Out of curiosity, what did you major in?

Target: Business administration. Nothing too fancy, but practical. I was always the one organizing group presentations—guess that translates to counting cash at the end of the day and making sure tellers' drawers don’t go a cent off.

Other: I can see that! Organization is half the job. How’s the team? Have you been mentoring anyone new?

Target: I’ve been helping out with the latest hire. She just started a couple of weeks back, fresh out of school herself. She reminds me a bit of myself when I started: enthusiastic, a bit nervous, but catching on fast. She’s already pretty good at handling customer questions—though the safe deposit box routine is still a bit of a mystery to her.

Other: Those boxes are tricky until you’ve done them a dozen times. Do you have a preference for handling the technical side or working face-to-face with customers?

Target: I really enjoy being at the counter most days, interacting with people from the neighborhood. But I also find it satisfying when a big batch of checks balances perfectly after a long shift. Most folks don’t realize how much of the job is about tiny details—catching an extra cent, making sure a signature matches, that sort of thing.

Other: I hear you. A lot of trust gets placed in those details. What inspired you to aim for this field in the first place? I know you could have gone so many directions after finishing your courses.

Target: Honestly, it’s partly because I enjoy numbers and routine, and partly because I wanted a stable job close to home. Being in the town you grew up in, knowing the people who walk in—that appeals to me. Plus, I’ve always liked being someone people can rely on. Maybe it’s because my father used to bring me along to the bank as a kid, teaching me how deposits and withdrawals worked.

Other: Family legacy, huh? That’s something rare these days. I know a lot of your classmates moved out of the area after graduation—was that ever a consideration for you?

Target: I thought about it, but sticking around meant I could help out with family stuff, watch my siblings grow up, and keep my roots. Plenty of opportunities elsewhere, but this town’s always felt like home. Plus, there’s a certain peace in settling into a community you know—kind of like main street in July, with everyone out and about before the county fair.

Other: That’s a nice image. Speaking of tradition, I know plenty of folks who had to navigate all sorts of paperwork to deal with residency or work status stuff. Did you ever run into that kind of red tape starting out?

Target: Not really, to be honest. It was pretty straightforward—job application, background check, and I was good to go. Nothing unusual with eligibility or forms. In fact, my onboarding process was a breeze compared to what I’ve heard from others who had to wait ages for final approvals.

Other: Lucky you! Paperwork is nobody’s favorite. I remember when I applied, it felt like every document had to be notarized twice. Out of curiosity, ever need to travel abroad, or have you mostly stuck around stateside?

Target: Mostly local, but I’ve traveled around the country a fair bit. Never needed to put together any complicated visa paperwork—just a suitcase, a travel mug, and I’m out the door. The furthest I’ve been is to see a college friend out in Seattle, but I always come back home.

Other: Sounds like you’ve got your spot in the world pretty well picked out. A lot of people would be envious of that kind of certainty. If you could change anything about your current role, what would it be?

Target: Huh. Maybe a bit more variety during the slow afternoons—sometimes I wish there were more projects to tackle. But otherwise, I like the stability, and the chance to connect with people each day. And of course, having summer birthdays means there’s always an excuse for ice cream breaks with the team. I look forward to those.

Other: That sense of camaraderie goes a long way. Have you picked up any interesting hobby recently, outside of work?

Target: I started playing rec basketball again with a group of guys from the old neighborhood. Each weekend, we hit the court behind the local high school. It’s not the NBA, but it keeps me active, and it’s a good way to unwind after a week of mental math and customer queries.

Other: That’s awesome! Do you ever get competitive?

Target: Oh, a little. Nothing like trying to bank a three-pointer and getting blocked by someone who claims they haven’t played since college. We’ve got a running joke: if you miss too many baskets, you have to buy everyone Gatorade. It definitely keeps things lively.

Other: Let me guess, you’re the go-to for organizing who’s bringing the snacks and reminding everyone when the next game is.

Target: Guilty as charged. Old habits die hard, and someone’s got to make sure people remember when we’re meeting.

Other: With all that handling of cash and receipts at work, I bet nobody in your group dares dispute the scorekeeping either.

Target: You’d be surprised—everyone thinks they’re right. But there’s something satisfying about writing the numbers down and knowing they add up. I guess that’s just my thing.

Other: For what it’s worth, I think you’ve struck a great balance between work and play. Would your family agree?

Target: I’d like to think so. My younger brother teases me for being too organized, but even he can’t argue with a perfectly balanced checkbook. My folks still expect me to show up for Sunday dinners and update them on all the neighborhood happenings. I’m the resident source for branch gossip and basketball scores now.

Other: Sunday dinners—now that’s a tradition worth keeping. Do you find yourself giving advice to other family members about budgeting or saving?

Target: All the time. I helped my sister set up her first account a couple of years back, and now she’s coming to me for pointers on saving for her own place. Having walked people through account paperwork at work for so long, it just comes naturally.

Other: That’s really nice. I think a lot of people would love to have someone in banking as a sibling!

Target: It comes in handy, especially during tax season or when someone’s confused about online banking features. Plus, every so often I get roped into helping out at career day at the local elementary. I get to explain what I do, and, I admit, I enjoy making numbers look a little less intimidating.

Other: I love that! Out of curiosity, if you could go back and give your younger self one piece of advice at the start of college, what would it be?

Target: I’d say don’t stress so much about picking the perfect major, and maybe don’t eat so much cafeteria pizza. Honestly, being willing to learn on the fly and seeing every interaction as a chance to grow helped the most. Plus, those late nights prepping for business finals taught me the value of teamwork—and coffee.

Other: Solid advice. Do you still keep in touch with folks from your university days?

Target: A few. There’s a group chat that’s still alive and kicking, especially anytime our alma mater’s basketball team wins. We try to meet up at least once a year, usually at the end of July for somebody’s birthday barbecue.

Other: Oh, so you’ve got other summer babies in the group as well!

Target: Yeah, it’s like half of us were born right in that sweet spot during summer break, when everyone was free to celebrate. It makes organizing a party that much easier.

Other: Perfect! Before we wrap up, is there anything you’d want from management to help you feel more supported in your role?

Target: I think some refreshers on the new systems wouldn’t hurt—especially with all these updates lately. Maybe some workshops or peer coaching would help smooth things over. Other than that, I’ve got what I need: good co-workers, reliable routines, and an endless stream of customers to keep things interesting.

Other: I’ll pass that along. Thanks for being so open. It’s always great chatting with someone who’s so dedicated and thoughtful about their work.

Target: Thanks, I appreciate it. Glad I could share a little about what makes the job worth sticking with.

Other: Enjoy the rest of your afternoon. Don’t let the Monday rush get you down.

Target: Will do. And if you ever come by for a summer ice cream, you know where to find me—right at the window, counting coins.

[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Target: Morning! Can you hear me alright?

Other: Hey—yes, coming through clear on my end. Thanks for hopping on early, I know you’ve got a packed schedule these days.

Target: No worries at all. I usually have rehearsals later in the day, so mornings are the best window for me. I actually love this hour—gets my brain going.

Other: Right, you mentioned you’d be busy at the theater this week. They keep you on your toes, huh?

Target: Constantly. Yesterday we were blocking a fight scene for the new play, and by the time I got home, my voice was shot. Occupational hazard, I guess.

Other: I can imagine. I’ve never had to memorize lines, let alone do it for a live audience. What stage are you at in rehearsals?

Target: We’re in tech now, so it’s all about lights, timing, costumes—making sure everything runs smooth. Last night we spent an hour just getting the right shadows during the climactic scene. It’s meticulous, but I love the details.

Other: The costume side must be fun. I remember you mentioning your director has a knack for vibrant color choices. Is this another high-energy show?

Target: Oh, definitely. Lots of quick changes, energetic ensemble numbers. It reminds me a bit of the shows I used to watch with my family on Saturday nights back when I was a kid.

Other: That sounds like a full circle moment! Did you always know performing was your thing?

Target: Well, not exactly. My parents will tell you I was always the kid making up stories in the living room, but honestly, it wasn’t until college when I really threw myself into it. Before that, I thought I’d do something ‘practical,’ as my mom would say.

Other: College theater can be such a game changer. Did you get involved right from the start?

Target: Yeah, I was in one of the orientation plays—nothing huge, just comic relief—but that opened the door. A professor encouraged me after my first-year performance, and I ran with it from there.

Other: That’s awesome. Sometimes all it takes is one person believing in you, right?

Target: Absolutely. Plus, I had to make my own network there. I was a little out of my element at first—everyone seemed to know each other already. But I found my people in the drama society. We’d do these late-night script readings and egg-tart runs—really brought everyone together.

Other: I’ve always loved that drama departments are so tight-knit. Your parents must be proud now that they’ve seen you go all in.

Target: Oh, they’re proud—if a little bewildered sometimes. My dad always jokes that he never expected one of us would be up on stage instead of in the audience. But my mom, she keeps every program and playbill.

Other: Supportive family is the best. You’ve moved around a lot, too, right? Were your folks born here or did you travel as a family?

Target: Yeah, moving was kind of our thing. My parents actually settled in the States before I was born, but they’d take me back to Manila every couple years to visit my grandparents. I grew up with Tagalog in the house, but these days, I mostly use it to call my lola on her birthday.

Other: I love that. Do you still celebrate the big holidays in the traditional way?

Target: Oh, for sure. My family’s always up at dawn making bibingka for Simbang Gabi. And Christmas lasts until January, you know how it goes. The food is the best part.

Other: That sounds incredible. Is there a dish you miss when you’re deep in rehearsal chaos?

Target: Hands down, adobo. I’ve tried making it in my tiny apartment, but it never tastes quite as good as my dad’s.

Other: Maybe you need to invite him to the next cast party! Switching gears a bit—how’d you end up in New York? Was theater the main draw?

Target: Theater was definitely the pull. After I graduated, I figured if I was going to give acting a real shot, I had to be where the action is. My first ever audition here I totally bombed—shaking like a leaf—but eventually landed a tiny part in an off-Broadway show.

Other: That takes guts. Especially moving to a new city. Did school prepare you for the madness?

Target: To a point, yeah. I mean, I learned a lot at university—lots of theory, some good stage experience. What they don’t tell you is how much hustle it takes day-to-day. You’re juggling side gigs and auditions, constantly learning. There’s a lot of “fake it till you make it” energy.

Other: You ever feel like you wish you’d picked something with less uncertainty?

Target: Maybe sometimes, when rent’s due and the callbacks are thin. But pulling off a tough scene or getting genuine applause makes it worth the grind. It also helps that my family keeps reminding me of everything I’ve already achieved. My mom is big on celebrating the tiny victories.

Other: I bet she is. Have you been back home to visit recently?

Target: Not since before the pandemic, unfortunately. My folks came out for my last opening night, though—it was their first Broadway visit. They got super dressed up, it was adorable.

Other: That must’ve felt special! You know, there’s something I’ve noticed—folks who train in the arts often have worlds of experiences outside the classroom. Any odd jobs before hitting professional stages?

Target: Oh man, tons. I did catering for a Filipino wedding planner—that was chaos but the lumpia was out of this world. Worked the desk at the library during undergrad, ran social media for a local restaurant. Honestly, every job’s a story.

Other: You must have some good stories from all that. Does any of it inform your acting?

Target: Definitely. Front-of-house stuff taught me how to read people—figure out if they want a chat or just the bill. Plus I picked up the best bits of different personalities to draw on for audition pieces.

Other: That’s such a resource for character work. Do you still keep in touch with your classmates?

Target: Some of them, yeah. Actually, we’ve got a group chat going, mostly to vent about auditions and share memes. One friend just opened a black box theater in Queens so there’s always something new happening.

Other: I think that’s the best support system you can get. Do you see yourself in New York long term, or dream of the West Coast at all?

Target: I’m pretty attached to New York’s chaos, honestly. But if a great film project came up out there, I’d at least give it a shot. The idea of more sun is tempting.

Other: Would you ever start teaching acting on the side, given everything you’ve learned?

Target: Funny you ask—I did assist a movement workshop for high schoolers last spring. It was a trip seeing kids just starting out, all nervous but totally game. I’m open to more teaching gigs, but for now, performing takes priority.

Other: A movement workshop! Was dance part of your own training?

Target: More like I learned by necessity. You don’t want to be the guy in the background tripping over props, so I picked up enough choreography to hold my own. My friend jokes that my dance style is “enthusiastic confusion.”

Other: That’s an image! So, between rehearsals, family, and all these gigs, you ever get time for yourself?

Target: I try. I’ll sneak away to the park, or catch a matinée. Sometimes I just hang out at a Filipino bakery, grab ensaymada and people-watch. Honestly, those chill moments help me reset before going back on stage.

Other: Sounds like you have a pretty full, vivid life! Can I ask—did you ever have to navigate any paperwork challenges when you were making the move from school to the city?

Target: Yeah, actually. There were a few extra steps getting the right papers sorted out for some gigs, mostly back when I was trying to figure out union stuff. It’s easier now—I worked through all the forms a few years ago, so I don’t have to worry about that anymore.

Other: That must be a relief. Sometimes the process can be daunting, especially when you’ve already got so much on your plate.

Target: Oh, for sure. I joke that the application essays back in the day were harder than some of my monologues. Staying organized pays off. And now, when I need a government ID or travel, it’s all pretty seamless.

Other: I respect that. So last thing, since I know you need to get to rehearsal soon—what’s your dream role?

Target: Wow, that’s a tough one. King Lear would be amazing, someday when I’ve got the right mileage under my belt. Or playing a hero from one of the Filipino epics—that’s the kind of part I’d wait a lifetime for.

Other: Those both sound epic. Do you feel you bring a unique perspective to roles that draw on your roots?

Target: I think so, yeah. There are little touches, things I grew up with or stories my family shared, that color how I read a script. It’s important to me to carry that forward, even if it’s subtle.

Other: That celebration of heritage comes through in your work—I’ve seen it! Before I let you go, any last tips for someone hoping to break into the industry?

Target: Honestly? Build your circle, stay curious, and don’t be afraid of the grind. And learn how to cook your comfort food. Nothing beats the taste of home after a long day.

Other: I’ll remember that. Thanks for making time, and knock them dead today. Can’t wait to catch your show.

Target: Thanks so much! Let me know when you want to come—I’ll save a seat up front.

Other: It’s a deal. Have a great rehearsal!

Target: You too. Take care!

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]
