Used to play in the alumni touch football league by the riverside park, but they canceled last season. I do feel sore if I sit too long, especially during long virtual meetings, but I try to remember to stretch. Occasionally, I get headaches, especially after my third cup of coffee, so I’ve been cutting back.

Doctor: Have you noticed any mood changes, like feeling down or anxious? Sometimes stress can manifest in how we feel physically.

Patient: I try to keep a positive outlook. There’s pressure to hit targets—my boss tracks everything on a big board in the office—but it’s nothing I haven’t dealt with since I got promoted. I get a little on edge during monthly reviews, but mostly, it's about keeping my team motivated. I miss the old family gatherings sometimes—especially the food and laughter—but I know I can handle the solo status for now.

Doctor: How’s your social life outside of work? Sometimes even just getting together with friends can help with that work-life balance.

Patient: I keep in touch with friends online mostly. Some of my closest buddies are actually from back in American Samoa. I message them about stuff going on here—like how the weather in Charleston can't seem to decide if it’s going to be summer or hurricane season, even in spring. If I visit, it’s usually for big family events, and that’s rare now. Here, I don’t get out much except maybe to church on main street or to pick up palusami from the little grocery over on King.

Doctor: It’s important to connect when you can, especially if you’re otherwise handling life alone. Have you felt homesick at all?

Patient: Sometimes. There’s not a big community for folks like me around here. Last month I went to the Pacific Islander festival upstate—they had some dances and a rugby match. Was nice to see the siva again, and I brought umu food to share. Reminds me of back home, though it makes me wish my parents could visit more often. They haven’t been able to since all the travel restrictions a few years back.

Doctor: I can imagine how that might be tough at times, being far from your roots. How long have you been here now?

Patient: Coming up on ten years since I moved to the mainland. The east coast has its own charm, but I still miss speaking Samoan daily. I call my folks every week, and every so often we talk about the old days: attending church, Sunday feasts with everyone singing and laughing. Now, the closest I get is trying to make oka at home on game nights, and that usually ends in me missing everyone even more.

Doctor: It sounds like you work hard to keep that connection alive. Regarding your job, do you have any flexibility in your schedule to take breaks or get in a walk during the workday?

Patient: A little. As the one supervising the team, most days I’m glued to my phone or laptop. The only time I get a real break is if a client cancels last minute or if I send my reps into the field and don’t have to troubleshoot immediately. Once a quarter, I take a day to drive out past the plantations—just to clear my head. Not much, but those are the days I feel best.

Doctor: That’s good to hear. It’s so important to find ways to step away, even briefly. Have you had a physical lately? We could do a checkup today, make sure there’s nothing medical contributing to your fatigue.

Patient: Last time I had a full checkup was two years ago at my company’s request. I remember because HR was on us about updating our health profiles. I passed everything, so they gave me a wellness voucher. My bloodwork was normal then.

Doctor: Great, but two years is long enough that things can change. How about any vaccinations or travel recently?

Patient: The last time I saw a customs checkpoint was right after my green card days. Now it’s mostly just local events—went to Myrtle Beach for a sales conference in January, but that’s it.

Doctor: Got it. Any allergies or chronic conditions I should know about?

Patient: No allergies. Only thing is my cholesterol was borderline last time, but that runs in my family. Mom used to tell me stories about heart problems back in Pago, so it’s something I keep an eye on.

Doctor: I recommend repeating your labs, as well as getting your blood pressure and cholesterol checked. I’ll also ask you to fill out a brief screen for depression and anxiety, since work stress can be a factor. Do you have any questions about these tests?

Patient: That makes sense. I figure it can’t hurt to be thorough. Honestly, after crunching commissions all day, I’d rather not face any surprises. Besides, the way my insurance is set up, I get better copays now than I did when I didn’t have all the paperwork sorted out years back.

Doctor: That’s good—having everything in order can save you a lot of headaches. Will you be able to take some time off if you need a follow-up or additional tests?

Patient: I have some PTO saved up. Haven’t really used it; there’s no big milestones to celebrate, and it’s always hard to step away when I’m the one making the schedules. Taking a solo vacation feels odd, but maybe I should try.

Doctor: You deserve time for yourself, even if it feels a bit strange. Whoever fills in for you, they’ll manage for a bit. Your health comes first. Do you have any other symptoms or concerns, maybe something you don’t think is worth mentioning?

Patient: Just sometimes a bit of heartburn, especially after spicy food. I keep Tums in my desk drawer. Otherwise, not much. Never smoked, barely drink except at big holiday gatherings.

Doctor: Good to know. I’ll make a note about the heartburn, and we can discuss diet adjustments if it continues. Since you’re on your own for meals, it can be easy to lean on quick options. Are you interested in advice for meal planning or finding ways to eat healthier even with a busy schedule?

Patient: That’d help, yeah. Especially if you know any tricks to make local comfort food healthier. Most of what I make is big-portion, family-style stuff—it never feels right making just enough for one, so I end up with leftovers for days.

Doctor: Sure thing, I can send you some resources tailored for singles, including ways to cut sodium and saturated fat but still get flavor. I’m happy to include some recipes you might recognize.

Patient: Thanks, Doc. I get nostalgic about Sunday family feasts—all those stews, taro, and coconut. I’ll take all the advice I can get. I try to keep my aunt’s recipes alive, even if it’s just me bringing oka to the neighbor’s July Fourth cookout and telling them how it’s done back in the islands.

Doctor: That sounds wonderful—and it’s great to introduce your neighbors to those traditions. Just a few more quick questions: are you taking any regular medications or supplements?

Patient: Just a multivitamin, plus whatever HR hands out in those wellness kits. I keep meaning to remember my omega-3s; they swear by fish oil in the health mags at work, especially in the sales department.

Doctor: Noted. Any family history of illnesses I should be aware of, aside from cholesterol and heart disease?

Patient: Pretty much that. My uncle back home struggled with diabetes after coming stateside, and an aunt had blood pressure issues. Everyone’s always reminding me to keep my checkups regular, or at least as regular as I can with my crazy schedule.

Doctor: Thank you for sharing that. You mentioned you sometimes get headaches and that fatigue sets in by afternoon. Any vision changes? Dizziness? Memory issues?

Patient: My eyesight’s held up, though I get temporary blurring after staring at the spreadsheet for hours. I should probably get an eye exam again. No dizziness or memory problems—I remember everyone’s quotas and phone extensions better than my own birthday.

Doctor: That’s impressive! Sounds like your memory’s sharp. Before we wrap up, do you have access to good healthcare facilities near you?

Patient: There’s a new urgent care that opened up close to where I live, out where the old cotton mill was. Most people in the department go there, though if it’s urgent I can drive into Charleston or even up to Columbia if needed. It’s not New York, but everything’s pretty convenient once you know the area.

Doctor: That’s reassuring. Let’s get you set up for bloodwork and those screenings, and we’ll revisit in a week or so to talk through the results. If you start to feel any worse—new symptoms, fevers, chest pain, things like that—please reach out immediately.

Patient: Will do, Doc. Thanks for listening. I appreciate you letting me ramble about work, family, all that. Sometimes it feels like I don’t get to talk about it much—outside of a sales meeting, anyway.

Doctor: I’m glad you did. Your health and well-being are important, and sometimes just sharing can help. Let me know if you need anything between now and your follow-up. And if you ever want a few more recipe ideas or to talk about ways to boost energy, my door’s always open.

Patient: I just might take you up on that. I’ll schedule the bloodwork before I head to the office. And who knows, maybe I’ll finally use some of that PTO—maybe even take a trip back home next year if things line up.

Doctor: That sounds like a great plan. Enjoy the rest of your day at work, and I’ll look forward to seeing you soon.

Patient: Thank you, Doc. Have a good one.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

test_texts:
[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Person: Good evening! I hope you can help me with a little dilemma I’ve been having. I manage a team at a spa, and lately, I’ve noticed morale hasn’t been the greatest. I’m looking for some creative ways to lift their spirits and get everyone back on track. Any ideas?
Chatbot: Good evening! I’d be happy to help with that. Since you’re leading a team in a spa setting, some morale boosters might include organizing a group lunch, introducing an “employee of the month” recognition, or maybe even planning a mini wellness workshop just for them. Could you tell me a bit more about what you think might be causing the morale dip?
Person: That’s a great start. Honestly, I think it’s a mix of longer hours and maybe a bit of cultural tension? We’ve got folks from all over, and sometimes it feels like people stick with their own groups and don’t interact much outside of work. Plus, balancing schedules has gotten tricky since our customer base grew after the Avurudu season.
Chatbot: Cultural diversity can absolutely enrich a workplace, but I understand how it could also present unique challenges. Have you ever tried incorporating something from the various backgrounds into staff activities? For example, potlucks featuring favorite traditional dishes or themed dress days. That way, everyone gets to share a bit about themselves. Do you think your team would be interested in something like that?
Person: Actually, yes, that’s a fantastic idea. I remember last year, one of my employees brought kiribath and pol sambol for a special lunch, and everyone loved it. Maybe we could make that a quarterly thing—each time, someone introduces the group to their own dish or tradition. Part of why I appreciate these sorts of initiatives is that it reminds me of when I first moved here from Colombo. I can see how it helps people open up.
Chatbot: That sounds delicious! It’s wonderful you’re willing to draw from personal experience to make your team feel more connected. Creating a regular opportunity for everyone to share what’s important to them could certainly break down some of those cultural barriers. Have you thought about bringing in language exchanges as well? Sometimes learning a few basic phrases in each other’s languages can help colleagues feel seen and appreciated.
Person: I hadn’t considered that, but now that you mention it, it makes a lot of sense. I often catch myself slipping in a few Sinhala phrases when I’m stressed, and it’s always funny to hear the team try to mimic me. Maybe I’ll organize a “teach your language” afternoon. Speaking of sharing, do you think team-building activities outside of work hours are a good idea, or should I keep it strictly during work?
Chatbot: Balancing work and personal time is important. Generally, after-hours team-building works best if it’s voluntary and not overly frequent. That way, those with family or other commitments don’t feel pressured to join. During work hours, shorter activities are often more inclusive. You could try alternating between the two to see what works best for your group. Are there any particular activities you’ve found popular in the past?
Person: Good point about family commitments. Many of my team members, myself included, like to get home in time to help with dinner or take part in family prayers. In the past, quick games or coffee breaks together have been the crowd favorites, but nothing too elaborate. For after-hours, the only thing that really drew a crowd recently was a cricket match we organized. Guess some traditions never leave you, right?
Chatbot: Absolutely, cricket matches have a universal appeal in many places! Keeping things light and familiar definitely sets a relaxed tone, especially in teams with diverse backgrounds. Since coffee breaks work well, you could consider structured “coffee chats” where two random employees get paired up to chat about anything—work or life outside—and see if new friendships blossom. Would you be open to something like a buddy system at the spa?
Person: That’s a clever idea. I’m always looking for low-pressure ways for people to bond. Some of my senior estheticians have been with us since we opened, and I think pairing them with newer team members could help everyone feel more settled. It kind of reminds me of my university days, when we’d get paired with someone in our faculty for group projects. Funny how some things stick with you.
Chatbot: That’s a great parallel. University experiences often provide valuable lessons about collaboration. Speaking of which, do you still stay in touch with any of your classmates, or draw inspiration from your academic days when leading your team?
Person: I do, actually. A couple of my batchmates from my business program have gone into hospitality management, so we swap tips from time to time. There’s always something to learn. I still remember one professor’s mantra: “A good leader always reads the room.” That’s something I try to do daily, especially during busy weekends when tempers can flare.
Chatbot: That’s wise advice. Based on your experience, what qualities do you think set a supervisor apart from the rest? Especially when it comes to frontline roles where you’re coordinating with so many people and tasks at once.
Person: In my view, empathy is huge—if you can’t understand where your staff are coming from, you’ll never motivate them. At our place, a lot of what I do is about making sure the clients are happy, sure, but just as much effort goes into looking after our therapists, stylists, even the folks who handle laundry. My days are a mix of scheduling, troubleshooting, and sometimes rolling up my sleeves to help with an extra massage or shampoo. There’s no room for ego.
Chatbot: That’s a very hands-on leadership style. Your approach must foster a strong sense of camaraderie. Do you ever face challenges balancing administrative duties with on-the-floor work?
Person: All the time! Paperwork and payroll never end, but I’ve found if you don’t check in with the floor at least a few times a day, you start to lose touch. Even simple things, like knowing who’s got exams coming up or who’s celebrating Eid next week, make all the difference. My wife teases me about the hours I put in—she says sometimes she sees me more at the spa than at home!
Chatbot: Sounds like she’s very understanding! Work-life balance can be tricky, but it must help having someone supportive at home. Do you have any strategies to make sure you also get downtime for yourself?
Person: Ha, I try! Sundays are usually sacred for us—unless there’s a staffing crisis, I switch off my phone and we go for a walk or make a big Sri Lankan breakfast together. There’s nothing like hoppers and seeni sambol to start the day on a good note. And if we’re lucky, I get to video call my parents back home in Piliyandala.
Chatbot: That sounds wonderful. It must be nice to connect with your roots, even while you're far from home. Do you find that your upbringing influences how you approach your work and relationships in the spa?
Person: Absolutely. Hospitality is in the blood for us, I suppose. Growing up, everything was about making guests feel welcome—whether it was relatives visiting for the New Year, teachers dropping by, or friends stopping in after school. Even here, I think those early lessons have helped me relate to clients and staff alike. I still get a kick out of seeing customers leave happy, even if it’s just because their nails came out exactly how they wanted.
Chatbot: Hospitality rooted in family traditions can be a powerful motivator. Your team and clients likely feel that personal touch. Do you incorporate any traditional practices or values when training new employees?
Person: I do. For example, we have a morning meeting before the spa opens, which is a bit like the way my parents used to gather everyone before heading out for school—just a quick check-in, to set intentions for the day and make sure everyone’s on the same page. Plus, I always remind myself to be patient with folks adjusting to the pace of the job, remembering my own first months learning the ropes in a new city.
Chatbot: That’s a thoughtful way to support new staff. Have you ever encountered situations where you needed to resolve conflicts between team members? If so, how did you handle it?
Person: More times than I can count! Just last week, we had a misunderstanding over break schedules. In those cases, I pull people aside and listen to both sides separately. I learned early on—perhaps from the negotiation skills we picked up at uni—that most problems come down to communication. Once everyone’s had a chance to be heard, the rest is usually just settling details. If all else fails, I make the peace offering—a round of milk tea!
Chatbot: Sometimes great leaders rely on tried-and-tested peace offerings. It’s impressive that you make use of the communication and negotiation strategies you studied. By the way, I’m curious—do you have any particular long-term goals for the spa or your career as a whole?
Person: That’s something on my mind a lot lately. I’ve been in the personal care industry for a while now, climbing up from junior roles to where I am. One day, I hope to open my own boutique wellness center—not just a place for massages or facials, but a space for community, where people feel at home regardless of where they come from. Perhaps I’ll even run some masterclasses for people coming from similar backgrounds as mine, who might not always see representation at the top.
Chatbot: That sounds like a meaningful goal. Representation can make such a difference, especially for those from communities that are underrepresented in leadership roles. Do you plan to offer training or mentorship programs for aspiring supervisors in your field?
Person: Yes, eventually. I was lucky—my degree gave me a solid foundation, but so much of what I’ve learned came on the job. I’d love to design a program for up-and-coming staff to shadow senior supervisors, pick up management tips, and maybe even get a taste of the business side of things. There aren’t a lot of folks in my community who get those kinds of chances, so I want to change that, bit by bit.
Chatbot: That vision could really empower others and diversify leadership in the industry. Out of curiosity, do you see any unique challenges people from your background may face when aiming for supervisory roles?
Person: Definitely. Language barriers, unfamiliarity with local workplace culture, and sometimes just the pressure of being far from home. Early on, I was one of the only men heading up a mostly female staff, and people weren’t sure what to make of that dynamic. But I found that respect goes both ways—show you understand the work and value everyone’s contribution, and they come around. Of course, there’s still the occasional moment, like when a client assumes I’m just there to carry towels, but I use those as teaching opportunities for the team.
Chatbot: Thank you for sharing so openly. You’ve navigated a lot to get where you are. Are there any resources or support systems you’ve found helpful along the way, especially when facing those challenges?
Person: I relied on networks from my university days at first—lots of WhatsApp groups and alumni meetups. Later, I joined a diaspora association here, which helped with everything from finding housing to job referrals. Now, having peers in similar managerial roles to compare notes with is invaluable. It keeps you grounded and reminds you that no one really has all the answers, even after years supervising a crew.
Chatbot: Networking really is a key component to growth. Do you ever host industry events or workshops at your spa for others in your position to connect and learn from each other?
Person: Not yet, but it’s on my radar. I’ve attended a few seminars and job fairs geared toward personal service professionals, and it’d be great to bring that energy closer to home. Maybe next year I’ll propose an all-day training event for other supervisors—bring in guest speakers who’ve made a name for themselves, and maybe even start a mentoring circle.
Chatbot: That initiative could benefit many. Shifting a little—what are your favorite aspects of being a supervisor? What keeps you motivated each day?
Person: Honestly, it’s the little victories—the smile from a client who just had her first spa facial, the way two junior staff bond over prepping avocado masks, the moments I catch my team genuinely laughing together. I love seeing people grow more confident, especially the newer hires. The little “aha” moments remind me why I got into this line of work in the first place. That, and knowing at the end of the day I made someone else’s job just a little easier.
Chatbot: That’s inspiring! It sounds like you create a supportive environment where people can thrive. If someone starting out in a similar field asked for your top piece of advice, what would you tell them?
Person: I’d say, never stop learning—even if you think you know it all, someone always has a new trick or perspective. And treat people with the respect you’d want, whether you’re cleaning floors or running the place. Titles change, but kindness doesn’t go out of style.
Chatbot: Excellent advice. Thank you so much for sharing your experiences and insights. If you ever want to bounce around more ideas or discuss leadership strategies, I’m here any time!
Person: I appreciate that, truly. This conversation’s given me a fresh perspective and some actionable plans. I’ll keep you posted on how the team responds—maybe next time, I’ll even have a recipe to share from our next international potluck!
Chatbot: I look forward to it! Best of luck with your team, and I hope morale soars. Have a restful evening and enjoy your next Sunday breakfast.
Person: Thank you! I’ll be sure to savor the hoppers and time with my better half. Goodnight!
[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Patient: Morning, Doctor. Thanks for fitting me in. I know it’s been a bit since I was last here for a check-up.

Doctor: Good morning! It’s good to see you again. No worries about the time—it’s important to stay on top of your health. How have you been feeling lately?

Patient: I’ve been alright, mostly. Been a little more stressed than usual, with everything going on at work and at the front desk. I think everyone expects me to have all the answers, you know? Phones ringing nonstop, people coming in, trying to keep info straight between departments and visitors—it gets a bit much some days.

Doctor: That does sound overwhelming. It’s easy for stress to creep up in that kind of environment. Do you feel it’s affecting your physical health at all? Any trouble sleeping, headaches, or other symptoms?

Patient: The sleep hasn’t been great, honestly. Hard to shut off my mind when I get home, especially after a day where I’m juggling, say, three calls at once while trying to sign in a FedEx delivery and someone’s behind me with a question about an appointment. By the time I’m on my commute home, I can’t stop thinking about all the things I might have missed or messed up.

Doctor: That constant mental load can definitely take a toll. Have you noticed any other issues? For example, changes in appetite, mood, or energy levels?

Patient: Appetite’s fine, I guess—maybe I graze a bit more than I should. Mostly pretzels from the vending machine or the hard candies we keep at the desk. My mood swings a bit depending on the day, but no huge changes. As for energy, I still get up early and manage the morning rush, but by noon, I feel like I need a nap. I push through since there’s always people coming in and asking for info, but it’s not as easy as when I started the job.

Doctor: That’s understandable. You’ve been manning the reception for a while, right? How long have you been at that position?

Patient: It’ll be twelve years this October. I started back when the office was using those old logbooks for everyone signing in—now it’s all tablets. It’s funny, sometimes I’m the one showing our younger clerks how to get back into the software if they get locked out.

Doctor: Twelve years is impressive! You must know the ins and outs of that office. Do you feel recognized for your experience and all the multitasking you do?

Patient: Most of the team is great about it, though sometimes higher-ups don’t really see how many spinning plates we’ve got at the front. Had to put together some guides for the newer hires last quarter, since our process changes so much. Guess I enjoy organizing things and being the go-to person for weird info, so it fits—I’ve always liked tying up loose ends, even back in my college days.

Doctor: That organizing streak goes all the way back, huh? Did you study something related to administration or management?

Patient: I did, actually. I went to school up the road not far from the Inner Harbor—majored in communications. Four-year college, lots of group projects and presentations. Back then, I thought I’d end up more behind the scenes, not right up front, but I do like chatting with visitors. Dealing with logistics came in handy in school and at work.

Doctor: Having those communication skills must make things smoother. Do you ever feel the urge to go back for more schooling, or are you happy with where you landed?

Patient: Sometimes I think about it, especially when I’m training the new folks. But honestly, after four years of tuition and all those term papers, I’m good for now. Plus, our office always sends us to workshops or webinars, so I feel like I keep my skills fresh that way. I still keep my diploma on the hallway shelf at home, a little nod to the effort I put in, you know?

Doctor: Absolutely. It’s good to appreciate your accomplishments. Can I ask—has your family background influenced your career path or your approach to the job?

Patient: For sure. My folks both worked steady jobs, always taught me to be dependable and work hard. Never missed a day at school unless I was really sick. Grew up nearby—never really pictured myself living anywhere too far from where I started. My whole extended family is in this part of the East Coast.

Doctor: That hometown connection is valuable. I think you mentioned before you’re living not too far from the Chesapeake, right?

Patient: Yeah, right outside Baltimore. If I leave for work before 7, I miss most of the traffic hugging the beltway. It’s gotten more congested lately, but I still prefer the suburbs to the city. I can be at Camden Yards in less than half an hour if the Orioles are playing a weeknight game and the weather’s nice.

Doctor: That’s convenient—I imagine you catch a few games when you can. So your commute isn’t too bad then?

Patient: Not really, though last winter we had a freak early morning snow—I ended up stuck on 95 for two hours. But honestly, I’m glad not to deal with the DC Metro or parkway traffic. Maryland’s home for me. I’ve always felt settled here—between weekends walking around the harbor or heading east for crabs in the summer, it’s hard to imagine living elsewhere. Plus, when graduation rolled around back in the day, all my family could attend without any crazy flights. Local pride, I guess.

Doctor: Sounds like you’re part of the community in every sense. And it seems your role at work sets you up as a familiar face for a lot of people—especially with that long tenure. Do you feel supported by your colleagues with your recent stress?

Patient: For the most part, yes. There’s a few who’ve been around nearly as long as I have, and we commiserate over coffee in the morning. Sometimes the younger ones see me as the office encyclopedia—“Ask Janice, she’ll know.” It’s flattering, but also adds pressure because I don’t want to let anyone down. Some days, I leave the desk for my lunch and end up answering questions by the vending machine anyway.

Doctor: It’s tough being the person everyone counts on. Since you said you’re having trouble winding down at night, have you tried anything to relax before bed? Meditation, or perhaps a soothing routine?

Patient: I started listening to podcasts—oldies trivia ones. I figure, if I can answer what album topped the charts when I was born, my brain might tire out. I’m not quite old enough for disco, but every time someone mentions Beatlemania or bell bottoms, it’s close to my era. My birthday falls on the same day Iron Man debuted in Marvel Comics—kind of a funny coincidence, right?

Doctor: That is a fun bit of trivia! So you draw some relaxation from nostalgia and music. In terms of your stress management at work, have you had a chance to delegate, or take any days off for yourself?

Patient: I took an extra long weekend last October, right around when the trees started turning. I try to save up leave so I can have at least a day off when my birthday comes every fall. With the new fiscal year starting every October, sometimes it’s tricky to get that time, but I make it a tradition. I turned the big 5-5 last year, so I told myself, “If you’ve been here over a decade and you’re eligible for AARP mailers, you get your birthday off.”

Doctor: That’s an excellent attitude! Fifty-five is a milestone. So your birthday is right as autumn really sets in?

Patient: Exactly. It’s after the summer has wrapped up, but before the holiday rush begins—just when pumpkin patches and apple festivals pop up around here. This past birthday, I treated myself to a small get-together with a few friends after work. It’s nice to have a break before flu season picks up.

Doctor: Sounds like you’ve got those seasons down to a science. You mentioned you sometimes train new employees—do you find mentoring others rewarding, or is it just one more thing on your plate?

Patient: Both, honestly. I get satisfaction from seeing someone grow into the job, but sometimes I wonder if I could use a mentor myself for navigating the mountain of calls and forms. I end up being a sounding board for all sorts of office drama—everything from password resets to “My lunch is missing from the fridge.” It’s all in a day’s work, though. Plus, it keeps me on my toes.

Doctor: I can see how the emotional aspect is just as draining as the multitasking. Have you found time to engage in activities outside of work that help you distress? Maybe something social, or just for yourself?

Patient: I started going to trivia nights at a local bar in Towson with some friends from college. We try to go every few months, and I’m the default team captain since someone needs to keep track of the score sheets and hand out assigned categories. Growing up in a household that valued education, I feel like I’m still putting all those group projects from university to use, just in a more relaxed way. It’s fun, especially when there’s a category about Maryland history—I usually ace those.

Doctor: That’s great! And having a connection to your college friends adds to the sense of belonging. Let’s circle back to your health: aside from sleep issues, are there any ongoing conditions we should check today? Heart, blood pressure, or anything related to your family medical history?

Patient: Dad had high blood pressure later in life, so I try to keep an eye on mine. Haven’t noticed anything out of the ordinary, but I’ve been a bit more aware since hitting fifty-five. I had a routine panel done at work six months ago—everything looked fine, but happy to do another. Mom always insisted I see a doctor in the fall and spring. Just trying to keep up the tradition.

Doctor: We can definitely update those labs and check your blood pressure today. Given your busy workday at the reception, do you get much exercise?

Patient: More than you’d think. I’m walking back and forth between the lobby, breakroom, and filing cabinets half the day. Plus, on weekends, my neighbor and I do a loop around the local park. Some days, that’s the only time I get away from being the answer-person for a while.

Doctor: Exercise and some fresh air—a good combination. One last question: have you had all your recommended screenings? Colonoscopy, mammogram, vaccinations?

Patient: Yep, I’m up to date. I’m pretty methodical about keeping tabs—my reminder file is color-coded, same as my incoming delivery log at work. The team at the health center here makes it easy, and my insurance through work covers most of it. I even convinced two coworkers to schedule their screenings after I did. I guess that’s my inner administrator coming out again.

Doctor: That’s excellent—being proactive is key. Are there any other health concerns or questions you have for today?

Patient: Nothing specific, just want to make sure I’m on track. I’ve always been one to keep things in order, whether it’s an appointment reminder or a visitor sign-in sheet. I figure, staying organized with my health is just as important.

Doctor: That’s a great approach. We’ll check your vitals and order your routine labs today. Try to carve out time for yourself and keep up with the relaxing activities. And don’t hesitate to ask for support—at work or here. We’re here for you.

Patient: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate it. I’ll keep the puzzles and oldies music going for bedtime and take that birthday day off again this fall. Maybe next time I’ll bring a trivia question to stump you.

Doctor: I’d look forward to it! Take care, and see you soon.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Target: Morning, Sergeant Lee. Appreciate you making time for this check-in. I just finished the video call briefing with Pacific Command.

Other: No problem. Always good to catch up and stay on top of logistics. How’s the rotation feeling this time around on base?

Target: Pretty smooth, considering. The humidity’s no joke, but it beats being stuck at a desk somewhere else. Plus, supply chain has actually been pretty decent out here so I can’t complain. How are things on your end?

Other: About the same, but it’s getting busier every week. I wanted to talk to you about your upcoming online course credits, especially as we look at the next deployment window. Do you have enough flexibility in your schedule to continue classes?

Target: Yeah, the courses I’m taking are asynchronous, so between training blocks and night shifts, I squeeze them in where I can. Sometimes I’ll catch myself writing an essay while on standby for inspections. But as you know, accreditation stuff drags on, and I haven’t technically graduated yet, despite all the completed credits.

Other: That takes some serious discipline. A lot of folks let it slide with the tempo we have. Are you getting any pressure to finish or just enjoying the learning?

Target: My folks check in about it, but they’re happy I’m still taking classes. Even if that cap and gown is, let’s just say, optimistically distant. Honestly, the coursework’s been a way to keep my brain sharp between field days. Quantitative reasoning last quarter almost broke me, though—I’m more of a hands-on, tactical problem solver, not much for abstract math.

Other: That makes sense. Sometimes the hands-on stuff is more useful out here than anything in a textbook anyway. Are you planning to stick with the same major, or are you looking at shifting gears?

Target: I'm exploring some electives outside my core program. Might lean into logistics instead of management—you know, something that lines up more with what I do day-to-day. I figure if I keep stacking credits, it’s bound to add up eventually, degree or not.

Other: That's a good strategy. You ever thought about using the tuition assistance for an associate’s, just to get something tangible for all the work you’ve put in already?

Target: I did, but the paperwork tripled when I tried to transfer my semester hours to the new system. Plus, I get moved around a lot compared to most students. So, I tend to accumulate experience more than diplomas. At this point, I’m in it more for the learning than the piece of paper.

Other: Gotcha. By the way, how are you finding the local culture and the people during your downtime?

Target: It’s fascinating. The communities around here are incredibly welcoming. There's a festival this weekend with a blend of traditions—one of them reminds me of things I saw growing up. There’s a certain rhythm to the island that’s very familiar, even if I haven’t lived here full time before.

Other: That’s interesting. I know some of the cuisine must feel like home, too.

Target: Absolutely. When I first landed, one of the porters offered me cassava cake. I nearly told him that I know how to make it myself, but it was a nice surprise. The coconut dishes here always remind me of my grandmother’s kitchen back in my teenage years.

Other: Did you ever get a chance to take a vacation anywhere else, or is it mostly service assignments and family visits?

Target: I travel mostly for service, honestly. Sometimes, our training takes us to bases that are just a short hop away, so if I’m lucky enough with leave, I’ll sneak a weekend and catch up with family in St. Thomas or visit friends who stayed on the islands. Makes me appreciate how the same ocean connects so many different places and cultures.

Other: I bet! That must shape how you see the world compared to some of the other guys on the team.

Target: It does, for sure. School back home was always a mix of languages and backgrounds, and now I see the same kind of melting pot here. I’ve gotten used to being the "odd one out" wherever I was—especially during potlucks, where everyone expects me to make pancit, even though my mom’s version is a blend nobody else has tasted.

Other: Pancit, really? So, your mom does her own spin on it? That sounds amazing.

Target: She does, yeah. It’s not the traditional Tagalog recipe—my family’s from a different background, so the flavors are unique. We celebrate the lunar festival, too, which always confuses some of the new guys who think it’s just all adobo or lumpia.

Other: That’s one thing I love about being assigned to diverse teams: the food game is unbeatable. Out of curiosity, is your family’s heritage mostly Asian, or do you have roots from other places, too?

Target: It’s mostly Asian, but not the big countries you’d recognize right off the bat. We’re from one of those groups that don’t get mentioned in most textbooks, so I grew up surrounded by languages and foods that don’t fit any particular box. Makes introducing myself at orientation pretty tricky—you should’ve seen the administrative officer’s face when I tried to explain.

Other: I can imagine that being tough. So, you’ve always had to sort of carve out your own path, both at home and in the service.

Target: Exactly. I got used to answering questions with “it’s complicated,” because trying to draw a tidy family tree just leads to more questions. But it’s helped me adapt anywhere I’m stationed. I know what it’s like to be learning the ropes wherever I go.

Other: Has that been an asset for the unit? I imagine being able to hit the ground running and blend in with new groups is pretty useful.

Target: Definitely. When we rotate platoons or need to coordinate with local partners, my background makes it easier to find common ground. Plus, the customs officers always cut me some slack when they hear me switch dialects. Comes in handy more often than not.

Other: That’s invaluable. How are you settling in with the team, by the way? Any issues with the new guys or senior leadership?

Target: No issues so far. The team’s been surprisingly receptive. There’s always that period where I have to prove myself, but after a few long nights in the comms bunker, you bond over instant noodles and bad coffee. I think some of them respect how adaptable I am, even if my path hasn’t been the most “typical.”

Other: That’s what matters. And don’t underestimate the value of your perspective. So, a logistics course next term and more field work. Anything else you want to focus on this year?

Target: I’d like to spend some time on professional development—thinking of picking up more leadership modules. It’d help if I ever move up in rank, and my chain of command keeps pushing me to take on more responsibility. But first, I have to make it through this month’s PT assessment without embarrassing myself.

Other: Ha! The last time I ran that circuit, I thought I’d never catch my breath again. But you always seem to handle the physical side pretty well.

Target: It’s necessity, honestly. Grew up around a lot of sports and physical labor, so I’m used to moving. Plus, being part of a unit means there’s that camaraderie—nobody wants to be the reason the team does extra laps.

Other: Spoken like a true squad member. I remember—even in high school, I was always trying to outrun my friends. So, do you get to participate in any ceremonial duties or mostly off-camera roles these days?

Target: A mix. I was flag bearer during last month’s change of command, which was a huge honor. Some of the new junior officers were surprised to see me there, but I think visibility is important. Not everyone who comes from a less-common background gets to represent, you know?

Other: It’s important for people to see that, absolutely. Do you ever share your story with other members who might feel out of place?

Target: Sometimes, especially one-on-one. A lot of recruits come in thinking they don’t fit the mold, but I try to remind them the military is bigger than any single identity. I’ll talk about growing up without a “mainstream” last name or what it’s like bringing culturally distinct food for lunch as a kid.

Other: That must help more than you know. Can I ask—do you have any plans after this contract is up? Any thoughts of moving back, or are you sticking with the service?

Target: It’s still up in the air. Sometimes I get the itch to go home, see those familiar beaches and hear the old stories again. But service brought me a sense of purpose and a chance to travel. If I stay, I’ll keep working on those classes and maybe train some new recruits. If I go, I might try joining my cousin’s business, which runs charters for tourists wanting to explore the less-traveled parts of the islands.

[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Patient: Good morning, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me today—sorry again for running a little late. Traffic on 40 was a nightmare all the way past the zoo. Anyway, how are you?

Doctor: Good morning! No worries at all, it happens. I'm doing well, thank you. What brings you in today?

Patient: Honestly, I wanted to have a bit of a check-in. Between work and everything else, I’ve been running myself ragged, I think. Plus, there’s been some weird chest tightness lately. Not pain exactly, but enough to notice.

Doctor: All right, it's good that you came in. Tell me more about this chest tightness. When did you first notice it, and what were you doing at the time?

Patient: The first time, it was a couple weeks back. I was at my desk, going over a client’s loan options—so, nothing physically strenuous, unless you count sorting through piles of financial statements. I just felt this light pressure in my chest, kind of like someone was sitting on it. Since then, it’s happened a few times, usually when I’m sitting at the office.

Doctor: Does it get worse with exertion or when you're stressed? Or is it random?

Patient: It’s weird because it’s not always linked to stress. Yes, it happens when clients are upset or loans don’t go through, but sometimes it’s just during a normal day. I guess I do spend a lot of time glued to my chair, with phones ringing and numbers everywhere. Maybe it’s anxiety or something from just being in finance for so long.

Doctor: Any shortness of breath, dizziness, or palpitations that go along with it?

Patient: Sometimes I get a little light-headed, but it’s usually after I’ve been at my desk for hours and realize I haven’t moved much. I haven’t noticed my heart racing or anything—just that odd tightness, and it kind of makes me catch my breath.

Doctor: Have you experienced any swelling in your legs, changes in your weight, or issues sleeping?

Patient: No leg swelling and my weight’s been steady. Sleeping’s been the same as always. I do tend to be up late, especially during quarterly reviews or if the interest rates get announced. There's always a client panicking about their mortgage. So, lots of client calls in the evenings, but I manage with coffee.

Doctor: I see. How has your energy level been overall?

Patient: I’d say I’m a little more tired than I used to be, but I don’t think it’s anything out of the ordinary for someone who’s been at it as long as I have. You know, sometimes I joke, “I’ve been doing this since calculators had big, clunky buttons.” Twenty-plus years of going over loan offers, running credit counseling clinics, always answering the same questions—it's rewarding, but mentally exhausting. Plus, I noticed that the younger folks in my office don’t really appreciate 90s music references.

Doctor: That does sound demanding. Just to be thorough, any history of heart disease in your family?

Patient: My mom’s side has a couple folks with high blood pressure, but no major cardiac events that I know of. My dad spent his whole life traveling, so I never really had full medical histories for his side—he always used to joke that my upbringing was more “international than most,” but he still took me to Cardinals games when we were in town.

Doctor: Important to ask—any tobacco, alcohol, or drug use?

Patient: I’ve never smoked, and I’m just a social wine drinker. If there’s a birthday party at work or the department has a get-together—like the one for my “last year before the big 5-0”—then I might have a glass. Otherwise, not really. Mortgage reviews don’t exactly pair well with a hangover.

Doctor: Any significant stress lately outside of work? Anything at home that’s worrying you?

Patient: It’s mostly job pressure, which I guess is to be expected. We're helping more people manage debt and foreclosures these days. Spring is our busiest season—everyone’s panic-calling to see if they can close on houses before Memorial Day, that sort of thing. Nothing especially big at home. My daughter recently sent me lilies for Mother’s Day, so that was a bright point.

Doctor: That's lovely. Remind me—any regular exercise routines?

Patient: I tell myself I should do more, but mostly it’s just walking around the River Market on weekends. If I’m feeling ambitious, I’ll head out to Forest Park with some friends, but between work and obligations, my treadmill has turned into a coat rack.

Doctor: I can understand how difficult making time for exercise can be.

Patient: Especially now—I still remember when I could stay up all night finishing reports and bounce back the next day, but these days if I don’t get my seven hours, no amount of coffee gets me through a client call. It’s funny, I was chatting with a friend over lunch last week, and we both realized this is the year we hit the same milestone as when “Jaws” first opened, with Spielberg. Weird sense of perspective.

Doctor: That certainly gives things context. When was your last physical?

Patient: I had a full workup a couple years ago, June of ’24, I think. Cholesterol was a little high, but nothing my old doctor was too worried about. I had a full blood panel done back then. Pap was normal, by the way—the joys of being at the age where those become annual reminders.

Doctor: Good to hear. When was your last mammogram?

Patient: That would be last fall, in November. I try to stay on top of things—after all, I help clients plan for the unexpected, so it’s only fair that I do the same for myself! My mother hounded me about it when I turned forty, and now I’ve got it on repeat in my calendar.

Doctor: Excellent. Any other longstanding health concerns?

Patient: I used to get migraines after international flights as a teenager. Not so much anymore, though. Actually, my daughter is going through the college application process, and the paperwork is wild—almost a throwback to when my own parents navigated the whole process in another country. I think helping her has been more stressful than any underwriting review.

Doctor: Any allergies to medications?

Patient: None that I know of. Penicillin and sulfa drugs have never been an issue; I joke that I’m as generic as they come.

Doctor: What medications are you currently taking?

Patient: Just a daily antihistamine this time of year. And a multivitamin because I swear, after a certain age, every piece of advice starts with “take your vitamins.” No prescription meds at the moment.

Doctor: Let’s do a quick recap. Chest tightness, mainly sedentary at work, more tired lately but otherwise healthy. Family history is fairly clear. To rule things out, I’d like to check your blood pressure and possibly order an EKG, given your symptoms. Sound good?

Patient: Sure, that sounds reasonable. I’d rather be safe—my clients come to me for peace of mind, so I guess it’s time I do the same for myself.

Doctor: Do you recall any specific triggers—certain foods, activities, or emotions that seem to set off the chest tightness?

Patient: It’s usually late afternoons, especially after back-to-back meetings or marathon sessions explaining APR to nervous first-time buyers. I’m already prepping for the summer rush, which starts around the anniversary of the tornado hitting Joplin, so the stress is always a little higher this time of year.

Doctor: That’s understandable. How long do these episodes typically last?

Patient: Maybe five to ten minutes. They tend to fade if I stand up and walk to the break room or get a breath of fresh air. My office has this big window over Main Street, so sometimes just watching the traffic helps.

Doctor: Are you ever awakened by the tightness at night, or is it only during waking hours?

Patient: Only during the day, never at night.

Doctor: Any stomach issues or heartburn?

Patient: A touch of heartburn when I indulge in too much barbecue—can’t live in St. Louis and not love ribs, right? But nothing persistent.

Doctor: Makes sense! Let’s discuss family history a bit more. Any conditions in the extended family, such as diabetes or cancer?

Patient: My aunt had breast cancer in her sixties, but she’s five states away, so I only know what my mom tells me. No diabetes that I know of.

Doctor: All right. Out of curiosity, did you grow up in Missouri, or did you move here at some point?

Patient: Oh, that's a question. I’m basically “from here” by choice. My parents took me all over the place when I was little—my mom’s Chicago roots, my dad’s career, which bounced our family between continents, embassies, and some pretty unusual neighborhoods. Missouri became home when I came here for college; I’ve been here longer than anywhere else. I joke that I have city loyalty, even if my birth certificate isn’t from the Show-Me State.

Doctor: That’s fascinating. Having a global childhood must have given you a unique perspective.

Patient: It did. And it made tax season wild, let me tell you. My parents would always pull out all those IRS forms for dual income, and the mess with picking which country counted me when. But it made learning to work with numbers come naturally, which helps in my line of work.

Doctor: I can see how that skillset would be useful in financial counseling and lending.

Patient: It’s second nature now. Closing on loans, helping folks sort out their debts, answering frantic calls when someone’s credit score gets dinged—never a dull moment.

Doctor: Thank you for sharing all of this. You mentioned turning a milestone age recently—do you mind if I ask how old you are? Just for the chart.

Patient: I’m fifty now—hit the big number last spring. Friends teased me because the day lined up with the Preakness Stakes last year. My daughter even baked a “golden years” cake, despite my protests.

Doctor: Happy belated! And your birthday was around the Preakness? That’s mid-to-late May if I’m not mistaken.

Patient: Yep, always just ahead of Memorial Day, round about when school lets out and the peonies blossom. I’ve never had to work on my actual birthday—one of the perks of springtime celebrations.

Doctor: That’s lovely. Thank you for clarifying. Has menopause started for you?

Patient: Yes, it’s been a couple years now. Hot flashes, especially during those summer closings with no air conditioning—but nothing too dramatic.

Doctor: Understood. Do you require any assistance managing symptoms or do you feel like you’re coping well?

Patient: Coping, so far. I read all the pamphlets, took my mom’s advice, and drink plenty of ice water. If it gets worse, I’ll let you know. For now, my bigger concern is making sure I don’t let work stress get the best of me.

Doctor: Absolutely. Let's try to manage your stress and monitor the chest tightness. I'm going to order a basic metabolic profile and EKG. If both are normal, I’d recommend regular activity—nothing intense, but consistent. And maybe taking some time to step outside during the day.

Patient: I can do that. I don’t want to join the statistics for financial professionals with burnout! Maybe I’ll even get a treadmill desk, if I can convince my boss.

Doctor: In the meantime, keep an eye on your symptoms. If you notice any worsening chest pain, shortness of breath, or if you ever faint, please contact me or seek urgent care right away.

Patient: Will do. Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate your thoroughness.

Doctor: It was my pleasure. We’ll get those tests done, and I’ll follow up with the results. In the meantime, do your best to fit in a little “me time” around all those client appointments.

Patient: I’ll certainly try. I tell my clients to be proactive about their finances—it’s probably time I start taking that advice for my health as well.

Doctor: That’s the spirit. Take care, and we’ll be in touch soon.

Patient: Thanks again. Have a good rest of your week!

Doctor: You too. Take care!
[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Target: Good afternoon, thanks for making the time to meet—especially on such short notice.
Other: Of course, happy to connect. I hope the connection’s clear on your end?
Target: Crystal clear. The only interruption I might get is if the base decides to start another drill. They’ve been on a roll recently.
Other: Oh, that must keep your days unpredictable! I always wondered what it’s like to work in such an environment.
Target: It certainly keeps me on my toes. There's this constant sense of readiness, but I guess I’m kind of used to it after a couple of years. How about you? Any excitement on your end?
Other: Well, my biggest excitement lately was making it to the office before traffic hit. Not quite the same, I imagine! So, before we dive in, could you give me a quick sense of your schedule? I know your job can make your availability a moving target.
Target: Sure thing. My shifts have been pretty regular for once, which is a relief. Still, there’s always the chance I’ll get shuffled around if something comes up. My supervisor’s good about balancing us out though—especially with the younger folks just starting.
Other: That's considerate! Speaking of which, out of curiosity, how long have you been serving now?
Target: I joined right after I finished school—so, still pretty new to the whole scene. It hasn’t even been three years yet, but sometimes it feels like a lifetime. Especially with everything that’s happened since COVID.
Other: I can imagine. So much change in a short span. And I’m guessing you didn’t have much downtime before starting, either?
Target: Nope—didn’t even get a gap year, just one week after graduation and I was in basic. The timing made for a memorable first holiday season away from home, too.
Other: That must have been tough! November birthdays must be tricky—right in the middle of everything.
Target: You could say that. Everyone's started prepping for Thanksgiving, and there I was, getting my first taste of MRE cake. Definitely not what I’d had back home in New England! 
Other: Ah, so you’re from New England originally?
Target: Born and raised. It gets in your blood after a while—clam chowder, autumn colors, shoveling out the driveway half the year.
Other: Connecticut accent coming out yet, or do you manage to keep it hidden?
Target: People say they hear it whenever I talk about pizza or tag sales. And don’t get me started on Dunkin’—it’s a very real thing!
Other: I’ve worked with folks from Hartford and New Haven, and it always comes up. Did you ever live around there?
Target: Grew up about midway between. Close enough that I could decide on a whim whether New Haven or New York pizza was better. Always got a different answer, of course.
Other: That’s the most Connecticut thing ever—an ongoing debate. You mentioned your first holiday season away from home. Was that just before you turned 18?
Target: Pretty much. I celebrated my 18th surrounded by drill sergeants instead of family, then my 19th at my first post assignment. Every year since, it’s been a new place or new people.
Other: It sounds like you’ve spent your adult life so far on the move, with a lot of milestones mixed in. How do you keep track of them all?
Target: I’ve actually kept a journal ever since high school. Helps to remember which November I was in which state. My spouse loves looking through it, actually—says it’s like having my autobiography already written.
Other: That’s amazing! Sounds like you have great support at home. How do you both manage with your schedule being so unpredictable?
Target: Lots of phone calls, honestly. We video chat as much as we can, even if it’s just ten minutes during chow. I got lucky—they’re incredibly patient and used to moving around, too. I always say it helps being married to someone who gets the military thing.
Other: Are they also from New England?
Target: They actually grew up in Mass, so we’re both used to cold winters and never agreeing about the Sox and Yankees.
Other: I sense some friendly rivalry! Have you celebrated many birthdays together, or is it tricky with your postings?
Target: We’ve managed a couple so far. One year, they brought a giant cranberry pie to the base just after my birthday. It was their nod to both Thanksgiving and our anniversary—which, by happy accident, falls right before Turkey Day too.
Other: That’s such a sweet tradition! So, between anniversaries and birthdays, November’s a busy month for you two.
Target: You could say November’s basically when I mentally hit ‘reset’ for the year. Lots of reminders on the calendar not to forget anyone’s big day—including my own.
Other: That’s relatable. On a professional note, since you mentioned the base and keeping a schedule, do you see yourself staying long-term?
Target: I’m still figuring that out. The commitment’s a few years at least and I’m only halfway through that. Part of me likes the idea of settling down someday—maybe buying a little place close to the shore, so we don't have to shovel as much.
Other: Connecticut shoreline, perhaps?
Target: Most likely. My folks still live close to the water, and my partner’s family isn’t far either. Plus, nothing beats the long summers at the Sound.
Other: Sounds like home never really left you. How do you and your spouse juggle holidays, given both extended families nearby?
Target: It helps that Thanksgiving and Christmas are right around the corner from each other—just a question of whose turn it is to host. My parents are big on tradition, but my in-laws can be convinced with good pie and football on TV.
Other: Football on TV solves just about every family conflict! 
Target: That, and a slice of apple pie, which is apparently the price of peace. It's become kind of a running joke—whoever’s team loses, they have to do the dishes.
Other: I like it! Speaking of traditions, is there anything you try to carry with you wherever you’re posted—not just from home, but maybe something small that connects you to your roots?
Target: I always bring a scarf my mom knitted—she says it’s for “weather like only we get.” Even got ribbed for it during my first winter on base, when it snowed six inches and nobody else was prepared. 
Other: That’s priceless. Your colleagues must appreciate that New England grit.
Target: They joke about it, but when the wind chill drops, everyone wants to borrow the scarf.
Other: I don’t blame them! So, apart from work and family, how do you unwind?
Target: If I have time, I’ll go for a run on the track—you’ll find a good one at most bases. Otherwise, I watch reruns of old Red Sox games or Facetime my partner.
Other: I see the New England theme again! Were you always set on joining up after school, or did you have other plans at first?
Target: I considered a couple different routes, but I wanted something challenging and steady. Plus, there’s a long line of service in both our families, so it just felt right.
Other: That sense of tradition must run deep. Did you meet your partner before or after enlisting?
Target: We actually met in high school—sat next to each other in chemistry. We stayed in touch even after I headed off for basic, and things just sort of clicked.
Other: High school sweethearts! That’s rare these days. So, have you managed to celebrate many anniversaries together, or is it mostly long distance?
Target: Out of all our anniversaries, we’ve only missed one being apart so far. The rest, we make work—sometimes with creative video calls, sometimes with a surprise visit.
Other: That’s wonderful. Do you find that the time apart makes the time together more special?
Target: Definitely. It’s never taken for granted, and we get to appreciate all the little details—like the first snowfall or just sharing coffee on the porch.
Other: Speaking of time, you mentioned you started all this after school. Out of curiosity, did you turn twenty last year or was it the year before?
Target: It was last year. My partner put together a little celebration over video—had my favorite snacks and even tried to find an MRE cake in my honor!
Other: That’s creative! And did you both get a chance to visit family together during the holidays?
Target: Yeah, we made it home for Thanksgiving. It’s always a big deal when everyone’s gathered, and my parents love having both of us back under one roof—even for just a day.
Other: I imagine it feels like hardly any time passes between then and your birthday!
Target: That’s true. Thanksgiving’s usually right before, so my birthday gets swept up in all the chaos. There was one year when it actually landed on the Monday before, which made for an entire week of celebrations.
Other: That must have been a memorable week! Did you do anything special this past November?
Target: We celebrated with both families at once—everyone made it, and my aunt made her infamous pumpkin rolls. It's one of the perks of having a birthday right before Thanksgiving.
Other: That sounds fantastic. You mentioned a lot of moving around with your job—do you get to pick where you’re stationed, or is it pretty random?
Target: There’s some say, but mostly it’s the needs of the service. So far, though, I haven’t strayed too far from home—which suited me for now, since I'm still early in my career.
Other: That’s lucky! Most people have stories of getting sent across the country. Are you finding it easy to adjust to military life?
Target: It’s an adjustment for sure, but the structure helps. I can still FaceTime my partner after shift, so that helps with the homesickness.
Other: Absolutely. Having that touch of normalcy probably makes all the difference. Speaking of, do you two have any plans for summer or is that all up in the air?
Target: Depends on the schedule, but we’re hoping to get a little beach time in. My partner really misses the shoreline, so if I get days off, we’ll be back down in the Sound.
Other: That sounds like the perfect break. As you think about the future—do you see yourself staying local or could you see moving further afield?
Target: Honestly, I think we both want to stay close to family, and Connecticut just feels like home. It’s hard to beat the seasons and the sense of community here.
Other: I hear that a lot from people who grow up there. Out of curiosity, do you ever think about what you’d do after you finish your service? Any second career dreams?
Target: Sometimes. I’ve thought about maybe pursuing firefighting or EMT work—something where the structure and teamwork would carry over. Plus, it’s the kind of work my folks have always done.
Other: Another family tradition?
Target: Yeah, you could say that. My dad was a volunteer firefighter in our town, so growing up I was always around it. And my mom's a nurse in Hartford, so service is just part of our DNA.
Other: They must be very proud of you.
Target: I hope so. I think they’re mostly just relieved that I’m close enough to visit, even if not as often as they’d like.
Other: It must mean a lot to be able to spend at least some special days with them.
Target: Definitely. Even if my birthday inevitably gets rolled into the Thanksgiving chaos, it’s worth it for the food and family time.
Other: You mentioned that was always “your week”—do your folks still make you a cake, or has that tradition shifted?
Target: My mom’s adamant about birthday cake, even if it’s after pumpkin pie. She says just because I was born right before Thanksgiving doesn’t mean I get out of a proper celebration.
Other: Moms are the best for that kind of thing.
Target: Absolutely. I just wish I had a better picture of the first one—my dad says the hospital was already putting up holiday decorations when I was born, so all my baby photos have turkeys and pilgrims in the background.
Other: That’s adorable! So you must have just turned 22 this past November, right?
Target: That’s right, and only now figuring out how to juggle a November birthday, an anniversary, and Thanksgiving all together. Maybe one of these years we’ll go all out with a three-in-one party!
Other: If anyone deserves it, you do. So, with everything on your plate—service, marriage, family—what would you say has mattered most to you over the past year?
Target: I think the last year really emphasized how important family connection is, especially with all the disruptions from moves and duty changes. It’s the consistency in the chaos.
Other: Wise words. It’s inspiring, honestly. Well, I know your time is tight; anything else you want to cover before we wrap up?
Target: No, I think we covered everything. Thank you for your flexibility. I should be around most of next week—the schedule says so for now, anyway. Unless we get pulled for a readiness drill!
Other: Noted, and I’ll keep an eye out for your message if things change. Have a great rest of your shift and enjoy those spring days when you get a chance to catch them.
Target: Thanks, and I hope you get some downtime too. Don’t let the traffic get you down!
Other: I’ll try! Talk soon.
[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

Target: Hi Emily! Thanks for making the time to hop on this call—I know it was a bit last minute.

Other: No worries, I was just wrapping up some emails. Glad we could connect. So how’s your morning going?

Target: Not too bad, although I can’t say I’m a fan of how cold it still gets around here, even in late April. Had to scrape frost off my windshield today!

Other: Oh wow, really? We’re already getting summer weather out here. Remind me again—where are you based?

Target: I’m just outside Milwaukee, so the freeze likes to overstay its welcome, if you know what I mean. It’s nice when the snow finally disappears, though—I get to bike along the Lakefront Trail again.

Other: That sounds beautiful. I’ve never actually been to Milwaukee, but I’ve heard the cheese and the breweries are legendary.

Target: Oh, absolutely. There’s always something going on downtown, too—Summerfest, Brewer games, you name it. Even if you’re not into beer, there’s always a good bratwurst or some squeaky cheese curds around.

Other: I’m sold. I might have to visit one day! Anyway, I’d love to hear a bit more about your current role and what you’re working on these days, just for context before we dive in.

Target: Sure, so these days I spend most of my time working with the analytics team at the company. Basically, I handle all the reports for our customer feedback initiatives. We’re doing some really cool stuff integrating survey data with product development.

Other: Sounds like there’s a lot of data wrangling there. Are you mainly remote or do you go into the office?

Target: It’s a mix. I usually work from home on Mondays and Fridays, but the rest of the week I'm in the office. There’s something about being in the workspace that helps me focus, y’know? Maybe it’s just easier without all the distractions from home—like my spouse asking for “just one more favor” during the lunch hour.

Other: Haha, I can relate. It always seems like the people closest to you assume you’re always available when you’re home. Speaking of your spouse, are you two doing anything fun this weekend?

Target: Actually, we’re celebrating our anniversary a little late. We both had work stuff on our actual date, so we made a reservation for this Saturday instead. We’ll probably go to that Italian place near the lake, the one with the amazing homemade pasta. Not as exciting as going on a big trip, but after a few years of marriage, you learn to cherish the small, cozy moments.

Other: Happy belated anniversary! Homemade pasta sounds like the perfect way to celebrate. How long have you been together now, if you don’t mind me asking?

Target: Let’s see... We tied the knot just before the pandemic hit, so it’s been a little over five years now. Feels like a lifetime and no time at all, if that makes sense.

Other: That’s wonderful. I know so many people who had their weddings affected by those lockdowns. Did you have to change your plans?

Target: Oh, definitely. We ended up swapping the big reception for a tiny courthouse ceremony and a Zoom call with family. Not what we pictured, but it made us focus on what mattered. Plus, we said we’d do a big party on our ten-year, so there's something to look forward to!
