Target: Sure thing. I start the mornings by checking urgent ticket requests that come through from the product team—they usually want updated feedback numbers. Then, I’ll spend a couple of hours cleaning the new data that’s come in from our customer surveys. Once that’s done, I use a mix of Python and Tableau to create dashboards. Then, I have recurring check-ins with my manager and the rest of the team. Sometimes, if a project is really pressing or there are meetings that would benefit from an extra pair of hands, I’ll end up helping some colleagues from another department—especially finance. It keeps things interesting.

Other: That’s quite a varied workload! Were you always interested in data and analytics, or did you come to it later on?

Target: Actually, back in college, I was one of those people who couldn’t decide on a single field, so I double-majored in psychology and computer science. I didn’t realize at the time how much overlap there’d be—understanding people and understanding systems. The degree definitely helped me land interviews, but I think it’s the combination of both perspectives that let me bring something useful to the team.

Other: That’s a great mix. You know, companies are always on the lookout for folks with that kind of background. Did you study nearby or go out of state for school?

Target: I stayed pretty close—ended up just across the state at the university in Madison. It was the best of both worlds: a big campus, but not far enough to get too homesick or miss out on Sunday dinners back home.

Other: Ah, Madison’s a fantastic city! I visited once for a conference and loved the vibe. The campus is stunning, especially around the lakes.

Target: For sure. I still try to get back for Homecoming if I can, and I have a few friends who stayed in town, so it’s always a good excuse to visit. Plus, I confess, I still have my old student ID stashed somewhere just for nostalgia’s sake.

Other: I’m now picturing you in full Badger gear, tailgating before a football game!

Target: Guilty as charged, though these days I’m more likely to be corralling a niece or nephew than leading any cheers.

Other: Haha, that’s life, right? Actually, this is reminding me—how long have you been in your current role at the company?

Target: Let me think… I started with the company just after finishing college, so it’s been about three years now. Started as a junior analyst and worked my way up to my current position. I’m grateful they took a chance on me right out of school.

Other: That’s impressive! It’s not always easy to get a foot in the door, especially in analytics roles these days. You mentioned working cross-functionally—do you see yourself staying on this path, or do you have other career aspirations?

Target: Good question. I think the dream would eventually be to lead my own analytics team. Maybe even branch out into consulting. But for now, I’m enjoying the learning curve and the chance to mentor some of our interns. It’s rewarding to see someone just starting out find their footing—kind of reminds me of what it was like finishing up finals and nervously looking for my first job.

Other: Finals—that brings back memories. What did you do to survive exam stress back then?

Target: Honestly, the big thing was coffee, lots of late-night study groups—and after the last exam, we’d all go for pizza at this spot off State Street. It was our little ritual every November.

Other: November, huh? That’s a tough time of year already, with the weather and all. Did it ever overlap with your birthday?

Target: Oh yeah, every year without fail my friends would try to sneak candles into some store-bought dessert during our study sessions. I can’t think of a single birthday in college that wasn’t a mix of lecture notes and confetti from someone’s locker.

Other: That actually sounds kind of wonderful—stressful, but memorable. Speaking of birthdays, do you have any big plans for your next one?

Target: Well, this year is kind of a milestone for me. I turn 24 in the fall, which still seems surreal. My birthday’s always right around election day, so celebrations sometimes get shuffled around voting. If I’m going out, I usually try to cast my ballot early so there’s no conflict.

Other: Wait, so your birthday sometimes falls on voting day in November?

Target: Exactly. There’s been more than one year where I’ve had my “Happy Birthday” sung in a line at the polls. Spirited Wisconsin politics, birthday treats, and chilly weather, all in one day.

Other: That’s pretty unique! Do you remember what day your birthday fell on during the last major presidential election?

Target: Yeah, I do, actually! I always joke that confetti at the polls was for me, not the winner. That was in 2024—I was turning 22, and my birthday landed smack on a Tuesday, just like the elections.

Other: That’s a fun coincidence! So fall and November have a special meaning for you. Any traditions with your spouse for birthday celebrations?

Target: We usually keep it low-key—I get to pick what’s for dinner, and sometimes we spend the weekend up north. Last year, we rented a little cabin near Door County and made s’mores by the firepit. Honestly, there’s nothing quite like autumn in the north woods: colorful leaves, crisp air, and watching a Packer game somewhere cozy.

Other: Football, s’mores, and fall colors—that’s hard to beat. Do you and your partner have similar hobbies, or is it more a ‘opposites attract’ situation?

Target: We have overlap, for sure: hiking, board games with friends, binge-watching sci-fi shows. I’m more of a reader, and my other half is into roller derby—so there’s always something new to try or cheer for. We joke that our wedding vows should have included “may your team always beat mine when I care least!”

Other: Sounds fantastic. Going back to your job for a moment—do you find balancing personal and professional commitments tricky? Especially with all the team and cross-functional projects you’re a part of.

Target: Definitely, it can be a bit of a juggling act. There are weeks where I’m rushing from meetings to dinner plans, or answering Slack messages while prepping for a family gathering. My partner’s job is customer-facing too, so some weeks are busier than others for both of us. We try to carve out time for each other—whether that’s a walk at sunset or morning coffee at our favorite bakery near Brady Street.

Other: That’s a good strategy. Managing work boundaries, family, and staying connected isn’t always easy. How do you decompress after a tough week?

Target: If it’s been a rough week, we’ll order takeout and I’ll disappear into a book for a bit. Sometimes we’ll grab tickets for a Bucks game or go skating downtown in winter—Milwaukee’s Riverwalk is beautiful after dark. Or just crash a friend’s backyard cookout if it's summer.

Other: You really make me want to move to Wisconsin! And you sound like you’ve settled in nicely there. Do you see yourself staying long-term, or are you considering greener pastures elsewhere?

Target: For now, I don’t see any reason to leave. I like the seasons—even the long winters—and it’s close to family. Plus, I’ve built up a great circle of friends and colleagues here. That being said, who knows? If the right opportunity comes up, maybe I’ll get an itch for somewhere with less snow… but I’ll probably miss the Friday fish fries.

Other: It’s good to have roots and routines. You mentioned helping interns earlier—do you have any advice for recent grads trying to break into your field?

Target: Absolutely. I always tell them not to stress if they don’t have their whole future mapped out right after graduation. I didn’t know I’d fall in love with data. Don’t be afraid to try different roles—even the ones that seem tangential, like customer support or operations. Those experiences provide the context you need for more technical work. And lean on your network—professors and classmates can open doors you didn’t expect.

Other: That’s practical advice. One last question, just so I can include it in the project notes: What’s one thing you wish you had known when you were starting your journey, from school to employment and beyond?

Target: I think I wish I’d known it was okay to let go of a “perfect plan” and embrace the unplanned. If you’d told college-me that I’d find my professional groove, get married during a pandemic, and get to celebrate a birthday at the ballot box—all before turning twenty-four—I wouldn’t have believed you. But sometimes, the unexpected turns out better than what you pictured.

Other: That’s really inspiring. Thank you so much for this conversation. I’ll make sure to include your thoughts in the project summary. And happy early birthday for the next “election season”!

Target: Thank you, Emily! This was great—let me know if you ever want any Milwaukee travel tips, or just to swap favorite s’mores recipes!

Other: Will do. Have a great rest of your day.

Target: You too—take care!

[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Target: Morning! Before we dive in, just wanted to say thanks for meeting with me. I know scheduling can be a bit tight right now.

Other: Good morning! No problem at all. It’s always nice to put a face to a name—well, virtually these days. So, I see you’re interested in some of the new weld inspection tools we rolled out. But before that, can you tell me a little about what brought you into this line of work?

Target: Sure thing. I got my start pretty early, actually—straight out of high school, back when “Bringin’ SexyBack” was playing everywhere and Blu-ray discs were new technology, if that gives you any context. Welding always felt like good, solid work, you know? Tangible. Plus, my uncle ran a small fabrication shop—so that was my summer gig through my late teens. Guess I never left the floor behind.

Other: That’s awesome! You must’ve seen the industry change a bit since then. What’s kept you in it for this long?

Target: There’s just something satisfying about seeing a project through, from blueprints to final inspection. Having your welds stand up under all those tests, it’s a good feeling. And honestly, sometimes the helmet gets heavy, but working with my hands is like therapy. Lost my partner a while back—feels good to stay busy and focused, if you know what I mean.

Other: I’m sorry to hear that. I can definitely imagine keeping active with meaningful work helps focus the energy, though. Did you two meet through work?

Target: Actually, yeah. She was training as a pipefitter. We met on a site out in Pittsburgh—crazy how sparks really do fly sometimes. She used to joke that all our anniversaries lined up with welding expos and trade fairs.

Other: That’s kind of perfect, honestly. Well, I’m glad you’ve been able to find some balance in the work. Switching gears a bit: do you primarily use MIG or TIG on your current projects? Or does it depend on the job?

Target: It depends, but lately, it’s been a lot of stick—and TIG when the steels get trickier, especially for food-grade pipe. Actually, last month, we had a bronze sculpture come in for repair and I had to break out the old-school gear. Brings me back to the apprentice days, when I was trying to get my first certifications. My hands still remember the routine—sometimes better than my head does.

Other: Nice! You obviously have some serious experience under your belt. Do you mentor new folks at the shop? I bet there are a lot of people who look up to you.

Target: I try to. There’s a few youngsters who ask a lot of questions about the craft and the art of a good bead. I always tell them, your grinder is your best friend—and never let anyone rush you, especially during inspection. I had a mentor once who reminded me to “weld proud and weld safe”—keeps me grounded, you know? Especially these days, with everything going on in the world. 

Other: Absolutely. And about the new inspection tools: do you feel comfortable adapting to new technology, or are you more in favor of the traditional tried-and-true methods?

Target: I keep an open mind, but let’s be real—there’s nothing like looking at a clean cap pass with your own eyes, feeling for defects. Still, some of the new ultrasonic gear saves a ton of time. When I started, non-destructive testing usually meant a whole rigmarole with test strips and X-rays. Now you’ve got handhelds that can analyze a weld in minutes. I just wish they were a little more forgiving of shaky hands—mine aren’t as steady as they were when I was, let’s see, just shy of twenty back in ’06. 

Other: I hear you. Technology keeps moving forward! Funny you mention 2006—I was in college then, so you must be around, what, forty?

Target: Getting close enough to where I start to lose track! I hit that big milestone last summer, in the heat—never fails, my birthday’s always just as the days are getting their longest, right around the end of the school year, when everyone’s itching for summer vacation.

Other: Ah, that sounds like a classic Gemini birthday! Did you do anything to celebrate?

Target: Just kept it low-key, really. I took myself fishing down by the Allegheny, then stopped for cake at my favorite diner. Used to always get a homemade one, but these days, it’s more about the little things. Never fails—my birthday lands right around graduation season. Funny enough, I graduated the same week I turned twenty, if you can believe that! Felt like I was born to toss those caps in the air.

Other: That’s a great story! I’m glad you treated yourself. So, about your background—you mentioned growing up working at your uncle’s shop. Is your family from this area?

Target: We’ve been in Western Pennsylvania long before I was ever around. My grandfather used to talk about steel and union organizing back in the day. It’s something that’s a big part of my family history—summer BBQs with neighbors, Sunday afternoons in church, catching little league. My mom was born down in the Hill District, dad came up from the South for work. Pittsburgh’s home, for sure. Nothing like hearing old stories of playing baseball under the Three Rivers’ bridges.

Other: That’s such a rich history. Do you find that your family’s roots in the area give you a unique perspective on the work you do?

Target: Absolutely. Growing up surrounded by folks who looked at steel and factories as opportunities—it gave me pride in what I do. And it meant growing up with people who looked like me making things happen, you know? I still remember the first shop I worked in, with a crew that felt like family. test_texts:
[START OF TRANSCRIPT]
Patient: Good morning, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me today. I know you had to squeeze me in.

Doctor: Good morning! No problem at all. How have you been feeling? Is there something specific you wanted to talk about?

Patient: Yeah, so I’ve been getting these really bad headaches lately. It started about two weeks ago, and at first I just thought maybe it was the altitude or the weather shifting since spring finally hit, but they’re not letting up.

Doctor: I see, headaches can be difficult. Are they concentrated in one part of your head? Any vision changes or sensitivity to light?

Patient: Mostly just this throbbing across my temples, sometimes at the back, too. And I do get a bit sensitive to light when they’re really bad, like I need to pull the shades down. I haven’t noticed anything else with my vision, but sometimes I get dizzy. It’s weird because it happens most often in the mornings, especially after days when I’m on my feet a lot.

Doctor: How’s your sleep schedule? Any issues staying asleep or waking up?

Patient: It’s hit or miss. My schedule always kind of depends on my clients. Some days I’m booked solid with appointments and stay late doing color or styling—other days I just answer calls from people looking to reschedule. Actually, lately, I haven’t been going to the salon since it’s being renovated, so I’ve been doing house calls for regulars and catching up with the training videos my company sends to our staff. But with the extra driving around and the late nights, my sleep has definitely been patchy.

Doctor: That sounds exhausting. So you’re balancing house visits for your clients and ongoing training?

Patient: Pretty much. With our salon prepping to reopen, my boss wants us up to date on the latest trends, so sometimes I spend hours practicing styles on mannequin heads at home. And when I’m not fixing people’s roots or trimming split ends, I’m calling suppliers to make sure our next shipment of shampoo won’t get delayed by the snow on I-70 again.

Doctor: That’s a tough commute! Have you noticed if the headaches worsen after those longer drives through the mountains?

Patient: Actually, yeah. Two weeks ago I had to do a big loop outside of Denver and up to Evergreen for an appointment. After that, my headaches really started intensifying. I was stuck in traffic by Floyd Hill, windows up, breathing in product fumes from my kit, so maybe that didn’t help.

Doctor: Hmm, sometimes fumes or fragrances can trigger headaches, especially for people in your line of work. Do you wear a mask or use ventilation when using hairsprays and such?

Patient: I try, but it depends on the client’s setup. At the salon, it’s easy because the air system’s great, but at someone’s house, I can’t always open a window, especially when it’s snowing. And let’s be honest, no matter how many times I wash my hands after braiding in extensions, the perfumed waxes linger for days.

Doctor: Good point. Have you noticed if there are any patterns—certain products or days of the week it’s worse?

Patient: Fridays for sure, because that’s when all the wedding parties want blowouts and updos. I go through so many cans of hold spray my fingers cramp. But since the salon’s closed for now, my headaches actually have shifted, which is weird. I expected them to get better.

Doctor: How about your caffeine intake? Sometimes we see rebound headaches if people increase or decrease their coffee.

Patient: That might be it! Honestly, the past month I’ve been living off iced lattes—one in hand by 7 am, another before noon. And then, since I’m not at the shop, I forget to grab lunch and wind up with a headache by three.

Doctor: Nutrition matters, too. Do you have much time for proper meals with your current routine?

Patient: I try, but it depends. My parents used to call every day at dinnertime just to check in, but now I’m either shampooing someone’s hair or in the car, so I miss those calls. Sometimes, before bed, I just heat up some leftover bulgogi I made on Sunday. My mom says it’s better than ramen at least.

Doctor: Your mom sounds wise! And those traditional recipes are probably much better for you than takeout. You mentioned your parents—do they live close by?

Patient: Not too far—just down in Aurora. We used to get together at that big Korean barbecue place on Havana Street whenever someone got a promotion. Lately, though, I haven’t had time to see them much.

Doctor: Family can be good support when you’re not feeling well. When you do see them, do you notice any improvement in your mood or headaches?

Patient: Actually, yes. Just sitting down for a meal, swapping stories about their early days in Seoul or how they first handled snow when they moved here—it's comforting. Sometimes I wish I could see them more, but life gets in the way.

Doctor: Emotional stress can certainly play a role. Have you traveled recently, or had any major life changes besides the salon renovations?

Patient: Nothing big, but with the new year, there’s always more paperwork. My sister teases me for being the “official form-filler” in the family—taxes, DMV deadlines, even registering to vote every couple of years. I took care of our ballots the last time we had an election.

Doctor: That’s a big responsibility. You’ve been a resident here for quite a while, then?

Patient: Yeah, I’ve called the Front Range home for years now. I still remember lining up bright and early at the rec center, holding all my documents in the biggest folder you’ve ever seen. Never been so nervous in my life, but the staff there were so friendly! Now I love hiking at Red Rocks and popping down to Boulder for the food trucks on Pearl Street.

Doctor: You’re certainly making the most of it! So with the headaches, I’d like to check if there’s any neurological concern—do you have any numbness, weakness, or trouble speaking?

Patient: No numbness, thank goodness. My hands get tired after holding a blow dryer for half an hour, but I think that’s just from the repetitive motions. Friends always joke that I should switch to massage therapy, but it’s hard to give up the color and fun of hair styling. You know, the satisfaction of someone loving their new look is kind of addictive.

Doctor: Occupational strain can definitely take its toll. Have you experienced any wrist or shoulder pain as well?

Patient: Wrists, yes—especially after back-to-back appointments. At least it’s easier now since I’m more in charge of my own schedule. But when I worked six days a week at the salon, without fail, I’d wake up with stiff fingers.

Doctor: Let’s look into some stretches you can do between clients to relieve tension. For the headaches, I also want to look at hydration—do you drink plenty of water?

Patient: I try, but with all the coffee and being in people’s houses—not always easy to remember. And sometimes I worry if the tap water tastes funny out here, so I stick with bottled if I can.

Doctor: It’s always better to drink more water, regardless. How about your time off? Getting any relaxation or just focused on work?

Patient: A little of both. Right now, since I’m not in the salon, work’s flexible. I’ve been binging K-dramas again—my guilty pleasure. Got sucked into one last night and next thing I know, the clock says midnight. That probably didn’t help my sleep either!

Doctor: Those shows are addictive! It’s important to recharge, though. Do you ever take a proper day off, or do you fill up your schedule?

Patient: I really should, doctor. My mom keeps telling me to join her at the teahouse in Cherry Creek for a proper break. You’d think with the Rockies right here I’d get out more, but when your work travels with you, it’s hard to leave it behind.

Doctor: I understand. These stressors can build up. How are you feeling emotionally, aside from the headaches and the workload?

Patient: To be honest, I’m a bit anxious. I want to make sure I keep my regulars happy while the salon’s closed, but not exhaust myself. And there’s always pressure—helping people get ready for job interviews or proms, people expect you to make them look their best. I love that part, but sometimes it’s a lot.

Doctor: Have you found it helpful to talk with friends or family about your stress?

Patient: I try, especially with my sister. We laugh about how we were the only kids in school with seaweed rolls for lunch. But she understands. We both help out at my parents’ shop sometimes, so she gets the pressure.

Doctor: That community support is so important. I want to make sure the headaches aren’t from blood pressure or something more serious, so let’s check that during your visit. Do you have any allergies or sensitivities to medications?

Patient: Nothing serious, unless Advil counts. I’ll sometimes take one for the headaches but hate taking anything unless I have to.

Doctor: Okay, we’ll avoid over-the-counter use unless absolutely necessary. How about your general health—any recent illnesses or infections?

Patient: Just the occasional sniffle. I got a sore throat after one long day, but it went away. No fever. I got my flu shot at King Soopers with everyone else in my neighborhood. Tried to sign up my mom, but she wanted to go with her church group instead—they made a whole outing of it.

Doctor: Good for you for getting vaccinated. Do you get regular check-ups with your dentist and optometrist?

Patient: Dentist, yes—I have a dentist I trust up in Westminster. Eye exam's overdue, though. With all the tiny braids and detail work I do, I know I should go soon. My vision hasn’t changed much, I don’t think, but it’s probably time.

Doctor: It sounds like you’re on top of your preventative care overall. Any long-standing conditions I should know about?

Patient: Nothing major. I had eczema as a kid, which flared up a bit when I started using more hair dyes. My parents always worried since their skin is a bit more sensitive, too.

Doctor: That’s good to know. For the headaches, I’d suggest starting a journal—write down the time, what you ate, your activity, and how bad the pain was. This can help us pinpoint triggers.

Patient: That sounds doable. I can keep it on my phone, maybe jot things down between appointments. My calendar is already a mess with appointments, but I can make it work.

Doctor: Great idea. While you’re in this transition period before the salon reopens, can you prioritize sleep and meal breaks? Maybe even block off an afternoon or two for yourself?

Patient: I’ll try, especially now that I’m mostly running calls from my living room instead of standing behind a chair all day. My cat likes having me home more, at least—she’s become the ultimate lap warmer during my breaks.

Doctor: Animals can be great stress relievers! One last thing: are you currently covered for health insurance, and do you have a primary provider outside of me?

Patient: Yeah, I get coverage through the salon. We all signed up as a group a couple of years ago. The paperwork was a hassle, but the HR lady walked us through it. My mom kept every copy of the documents, just in case. That’s probably where I get my habit of double-checking everything.

Doctor: Good, that gives us more flexibility. Is there anything else on your mind or any other symptoms you’re worried about?

Patient: Not really, just hoping to get these headaches under control before wedding season starts. Once we’re back at the shop, I expect things will get way busier. I want to be at my best—nobody wants a stylist with a headache!

Doctor: Let’s make that our goal. I’ll write up a summary of our plan and get you started with the headache journal. Drink plenty of water, try for more consistent sleep, and consider reducing caffeine just a bit—gradually, so you don’t get rebound headaches. And remember to reach out if anything new comes up or if your symptoms worsen.

Patient: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it. I’ll try the journal and update you, especially if anything changes.

Doctor: You’re welcome. Take things one step at a time, and remember, taking care of yourself helps you take care of your clients, too. I’ll see you at your next appointment!

Patient: Thanks, Doctor. See you soon.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]
